  1642  
  1643  D. Determination To Exempt Additional Products
  1644  
  1645      In addition to the products initially proposed for exemption in the 
  1646  June 5, 2026 FRN, the Trade Representative, in accordance with the 
  1647  specific direction of the President, has determined in each 
  1648  investigation to exclude an additional 471 products from tariffs 
  1649  imposed with respect to products of that economy. In certain 
  1650  investigations, the Trade Representative also has determined to apply 
  1651  additional exemptions for products from that specific investigated 
  1652  economy based on requested exemptions negotiated in the context of 
  1653  certain agreements and arrangements.
  1654      A number of comments expressed support for product exemptions in 
  1655  addition to the initial list of proposed exemptions in the June 5, 2026 
  1656  FRN. Comments requested exemptions of products including certain 
  1657  agriculture products; metals and alloys; chemicals; semiconductor 
  1658  manufacturing equipment; and art, antique, and collectible products. 
  1659  Certain economies that have concluded ARTs or similar arrangements with 
  1660  the United States have also requested exemption of products negotiated 
  1661  as part of those agreements and arrangements.
  1662      Having considered the public comments, advice of the Section 301 
  1663  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees, and the 
  1664  specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative 
  1665  determined to exempt the following additional products from the scope 
  1666  of actions: certain animal products; certain seeds; certain vegetable 
  1667  products; certain sugar and sugar containing products; unflavored 
  1668  instant coffee; certain fertilizer inputs and pesticide inputs; certain 
  1669  animal hides and leather; certain wood products; vanadium oxides and 
  1670  hydroxides; pig iron; certain ferrous inputs and waste; certain 
  1671  aluminum scrap waste; aluminum hydroxide; ash containing precious 
  1672  metals or precious metal compounds; certain battery waste and scrap; 
  1673  certain semiconductor manufacturing equipment; certain pharmaceuticals 
  1674  and pharmaceutical ingredients; worked shell; worn clothing; and 
  1675  certain antiques, collectibles, and art.
  1676      With respect to certain animal products used as food for animals or 
  1677  an input in such food, commenters noted that these products are 
  1678  incorporated into U.S. animal nutrition programs that support 
  1679  livestock, poultry, aquaculture, and pet food production. According to 
  1680  commenters, there is little opportunity for import substitution for 
  1681  these products and any tariff applied to these products would impose 
  1682  additional costs on U.S. consumers.
  1683      With respect to seeds of a kind used for planting, commenters noted 
  1684  that tariffs on seeds have resulted in increased costs for U.S. seed 
  1685  producers and U.S. farmers. According to comments, tariffs that impact 
  1686  seed movement erode the ability of U.S. seed companies to provide U.S. 
  1687  farmers with pure, high-quality seeds at an affordable price due to the 
  1688  global nature of seed production. Specifically, many U.S. seed 
  1689  companies have foreign operations to take advantage of environmental 
  1690  and production conditions, such as additional growing seasons. 
  1691  Commenters also noted that the increased costs associated with seed 
  1692  production could reduce choices in the marketplace for consumers as 
  1693  certain varieties of seed will no longer be viable for 
  1694  commercialization in the United States.
  1695      With respect to certain vegetable products, commenters noted that 
  1696  certain products falling under the relevant HTSUS subheading are 
  1697  already included in Annex A to the June 5, 2026 FRN, but that the 
  1698  proposed product exemptions are limited to products used for religious 
  1699  purposes only. According to comments, products in the relevant HTSUS 
  1700  subheading are essential growing-media and fiber inputs used in nursery 
  1701  production that have no domestic source, including coconut coir, jute 
  1702  burlap, and sisal twine. According to comments, the crops used to 
  1703  produce these products are not commercially grown in the United States 
  1704  given climate limitations and, therefore, there is no domestic industry 
  1705  capable of producing these inputs for the U.S. horticulture sector.
  1706      With respect to in-quota imports of certain sugar and sugar-
  1707  containing products, commenters noted that U.S. sugar producers are 
  1708  more efficient than ever and domestic sugar yields have increased, yet 
  1709  the United States has never produced enough sugar to meet its domestic 
  1710  demand. To meet this demand, the United States has historically had to 
  1711  import significant amounts of sugar. According to comments, U.S. sugar 
  1712  processing
  1713  
  1714  [[Page 47332]]
  1715  
  1716  facilities rely on certain in-quota sugar to meet U.S. demand and 
  1717  supply a critical input of the U.S. food supply chain.
  1718      With respect to unflavored instant coffee, commenters noted that 
  1719  unflavored instant coffee is not available from domestic sources in 
  1720  sufficient quantities for U.S. consumers and coffee companies, 
  1721  including value-added manufacturers. These comments also maintained 
  1722  that over 99 percent of instant coffee imports come from economies 
  1723  covered by these investigations and there are not adequate non-tariffed 
  1724  alternatives. Commenters also noted that U.S. coffee companies will 
  1725  continue to be at a disadvantage producing and innovating ready-to-
  1726  drink and cold brew coffee compared to their foreign competitors if 
  1727  tariffs on unflavored instant coffee are imposed.
  1728      With respect to certain fertilizer inputs and pesticide inputs, 
  1729  commenters noted that imposing additional duties on these chemicals 
  1730  could cause disruptions or shortages in the domestic supply due to the 
  1731  limited availability of certain active ingredients outside of the 
  1732  investigated economies and because these products cannot be produced in 
  1733  the United States in sufficient quantities to meet domestic demand. 
  1734  Commenters also noted that the exemptions would be essential to avoid 
  1735  tariff inversion, causing U.S. manufacturers who produce value-added 
  1736  products to be disadvantaged in comparison to importers of finished 
  1737  agriculture chemical products.
  1738      With respect to certain animal hides and leather products, 
  1739  commenters noted that certain types of exotic leather--including 
  1740  reptile and ostrich--cannot be obtained in the United States because 
  1741  there is no domestic supply. According to commenters, tariffs would 
  1742  cause the migration of exotic leather manufacturing and American jobs 
  1743  to other countries, such as Mexico.
  1744      With respect to certain wood and wood products, commenters noted 
  1745  that certain types of wood and wood product imports--including 
  1746  eucalyptus and certain eucalyptus products--are not available from 
  1747  domestic producers in sufficient quantities to meet U.S. demand. 
  1748  According to commenters, these products are raw material inputs that 
  1749  are used to make timber and crane mats necessary in U.S. construction, 
  1750  powerline installation, and heavy civil infrastructure.
  1751      With respect to vanadium oxides and hydroxides, commenters noted 
  1752  that these products are necessary critical mineral inputs for which 
  1753  there is no or insufficient primary production in the United States and 
  1754  additional tariffs on these materials would cause serious supply 
  1755  dislocations for critical energy-storage infrastructure including AI 
  1756  data centers, electric-grid resiliency, and defense applications. 
  1757  According to comments, vanadium and vanadium electrolytes are necessary 
  1758  inputs across multiple sectors, including steel (including high-
  1759  strength, low-alloy steels for construction, pipelines, and automotive 
  1760  applications); titanium alloys used in aerospace and defense; and 
  1761  critical energy-storage.

  1767  sources of pig iron were limited given that China consumes virtually 
  1768  all of the pig iron it produces, and supply from Russia and Ukraine has 
  1769  been affected by the Russia-Ukraine war. Commenters also stated that 
  1770  pig iron is an essential raw material for iron foundry operations, and 
  1771  that it is melted and mixed with scrap iron and other alloys to produce 
  1772  cast iron. The comments observed that there is no substitute for pig 
  1773  iron, and that additional tariffs on pig iron imports would exacerbate

  1775      With respect to certain ferrous products, including pellets, 
  1776  turnings, shavings, chips, fillings, trimmings, and stampings,

  1781  carbon and alloy steel production, and there is no viable domestic 
  1782  supply for these products.
  1783      With respect to aluminum scrap and waste, commenters noted it is 
  1784  key feedstock material for the U.S. aluminum industry and imposing 
  1785  tariffs would disrupt the supply chains, negatively impacting U.S. 
  1786  aluminum production and, in turn, harming downstream industries and the 
  1787  U.S. economy.
  1788      With respect to aluminum hydroxide, commenters noted that the sole 
  1789  U.S. supplier of aluminum hydroxide is unable to meet U.S. demand and 
  1790  that approximately 40 percent of U.S. supply is sourced from Brazil, 
  1791  with remaining supply supported by producers in Germany and 
  1792  T[uuml]rkiye, among others. According to comments, aluminum hydroxide 
  1793  is an essential, non-substitutable raw material used in critical 
  1794  applications such as sanitation of drinking water, production of flame-
  1795  retardant polymer materials used in defense and industrial 
  1796  applications, production of oil and gas, and refining of aluminum. 
  1797  Companies that use aluminum hydroxide in these and other applications 
  1798  require a stable and cost-effective supply of aluminum hydroxide.
  1799      With respect to ash containing precious metals or precious metal 
  1800  compounds, commenters noted that tariffs on these items would increase 
  1801  costs and disrupt supply chains for products needed to protect U.S. 
  1802  national security, U.S. critical mineral security, and medical device 
  1803  supply chains.
  1804      With respect to certain battery waste and scrap, commenters noted 
  1805  that these products, which are crucial inputs for, among other things, 
  1806  communications and safety technologies, are not available from U.S. 
  1807  manufacturers in sufficient quantities or at commercially reasonable 
  1808  prices. Commenters also noted additional tariffs on these products 
  1809  would result in significant supply chain dislocations by increasing 
  1810  costs, reducing sourcing flexibility, delaying production schedules, 
  1811  and limiting product availability.
  1812      With respect to certain semiconductor manufacturing equipment, 
  1813  commenters noted that these highly specialized tools are not readily 
  1814  substitutable, and that applying Section 301 tariffs to these products 
  1815  would increase investment costs for U.S. manufacturing without 
  1816  materially encouraging the investigated economies to eliminate the 
  1817  acts, policies, and practices determined to be actionable in the 
  1818  investigations. The comments noted that these items are like other 
  1819  products already proposed for exemption.
  1820      With respect to pharmaceuticals and pharmaceutical ingredients, 
  1821  commenters suggested that these products are ingredients that support 
  1822  U.S. manufacturing and cannot be obtained in the United States. 
  1823  Comments further observed that these products were used for health 
  1824  purposes similar to uses for products already proposed for exemption 
  1825  from tariffs.
  1826      With respect to worked shell, commenters noted that there is no 
  1827  U.S. source that can sufficiently meet domestic demand.
  1828      With respect to used worn clothing, and other worn articles, 
  1829  commenters noted that the secondhand apparel market, which is now a 
  1830  mainstream market, has distinct commercial characteristics in 
  1831  comparison to the
  1832  
  1833  [[Page 47333]]
  1834  
  1835  broader retail apparel market, and that the used clothing market is 
  1836  structurally different from new, commercially manufactured clothing. 
  1837  Commenters also noted that additional Section 301 tariffs on used 
  1838  clothing would undermine the goal of eliminating the investigated acts, 
  1839  policies, and practices of the investigated economies; be 
  1840  disproportionate to the value of the goods themselves (i.e., the 
  1841  additional tariffs would be on the resale of the good, not its 
  1842  production); cause serious dislocations in consumer access to

  1845      With respect to certain goods under HTSUS Chapter 97, including, 
  1846  among other things, art, antiques, and collections and collectors' 
  1847  pieces of numismatic interest; goods of zoological, botanical, 
  1848  mineralogical, anatomical interest; extinct or endangered species and 
  1849  parts thereof; and goods of archeological, ethnographic or historical 
  1850  interest, commenters emphasized the unique quality, design, history, 
  1851  sourcing or origin, and supply chains of certain works of art and

  1880  the investigations.
  1881      The Trade Representative has also determined, consistent with the 
  1882  specific direction of the President, to exempt certain products of 
  1883  Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, the European 
  1884  Union, Guatemala, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Switzerland, Taiwan, and 
  1885  the United Kingdom from the tariffs imposed on products of that economy 
  1886  in each respective investigation. Exempting these products would be 
  1887  appropriate to encourage each economy to fulfill its commitments 
  1888  regarding forced labor import prohibitions in its ART or, in the case 
  1889  of the European Union, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom, would be 
  1890  appropriate to encourage the economy to impose and effectively enforce 
  1891  a forced labor import prohibition.
  1892  
  1893  E. Determination Not To Exempt Additional Products and Response to 
  1894  Comments
  1895  
  1896      USTR received numerous comments that requested that additional 
  1897  products be added to the exemption list and exempted from tariffs. 
  1898  These comments covered products in a wide range of industries. Most 
  1899  comments that requested that particular products be added to the 
  1900  exemption list based their request on six arguments. These included: 
  1901  (1) requested products have limited or no availability from U.S. 
  1902  source; (2) additional tariffs would increase costs for producers and 
  1903  consumers; (3) tariffs are a competitive disadvantage for U.S. 
  1904  businesses; (4) products requested for exemption are unrelated to the 
  1905  acts, policies, and practices investigated; (5) tariffs would not shift 
  1906  production to the United States; and (6) the tariffs would cause 
  1907  economy-wide disruptions. These six arguments are discussed below, 
  1908  followed by a response to those arguments.
  1909      Products have limited or no availability from U.S. sources. A large 
  1910  number of comments requested the exemption of products due to limited 
  1911  or no availability from domestic sources. These products included 
  1912  medical devices, decorations, frozen seafood, beads, hats, refined 
  1913  lead, olive oil, packaging products, travel products, and sporting 
  1914  goods.
  1915      Several comments noted that domestic producers supplied only a 
  1916  small portion of U.S. demand or were unable to meet all of domestic 
  1917  demand. Comments also noted that their products were not available from 
  1918  domestic sources at reasonable prices or domestic production was not 
  1919  commercially viable, as no domestic producer has the production 
  1920  capacity, specialized equipment, technical expertise, or quality 
  1921  systems necessary to supply the domestic market. Due to the lack of 
  1922  domestic sources, some comments noted that companies would be forced to 
  1923  curtail their business. Additionally, some comments noted that because 
  1924  so many economies would be covered by the tariffs, it would not be 
  1925  possible to shift production to economies not subject to the tariffs 
  1926  and doing so would require significant time and investment.
  1927      Increased costs. Numerous comments reported that the tariffs would 
  1928  result in increased costs to U.S. companies and consumers. These 
  1929  comments came from a range of industries, including: sugar, travel 
  1930  bags, agricultural packaging products, food products, parts and 
  1931  accessories for inkjet printing, and auto parts.
  1932      Comments noted that due to limited domestic availability, costs 
  1933  would increase for U.S. supply chains, including for U.S. food and U.S. 
  1934  manufacturing. Comments noted increasing production costs would result 
  1935  in a reduction in U.S. investment and the funds necessary to create 
  1936  conditions of fair trade, including responsible labor practices. 
  1937  Commenters also suggested that the increased costs would impact 
  1938  retailers, small businesses, and consumers. A comment regarding parts 
  1939  and accessories for inkjet printing systems reported that the tariffs 
  1940  would increase operating and maintenance costs for U.S. companies, 
  1941  extend repair times, disrupt production, and reduce the competitiveness 
  1942  of U.S. manufacturers. Similarly, a comment on auto parts noted that as 
  1943  a result of the tariffs, U.S. distributors, repair shops, and consumers 
  1944  would face higher prices, reduced product availability, and diminished 
  1945  competitiveness in the aftermarket supply chain.
  1946      Competitive disadvantage for U.S. businesses. Comments from a 
  1947  variety of industries noted that tariffs put products produced in the 
  1948  United States at a competitive disadvantage domestically and in 
  1949  international markets. With respect to agricultural and horticultural
  1950  
  1951  [[Page 47334]]
  1952  
  1953  products, for example, commenters noted that they rely upon imports to 
  1954  operate efficiently and remain competitive. Similarly, a comment 
  1955  regarding imports of goose down used in domestic production noted that 
  1956  tariffs on the raw materials will increase costs on domestic 
  1957  manufacturing, making their products less accessible to U.S. consumers. 
  1958  A global producer of electric bicycles that assembles bicycles in the 
  1959  United States using certain imported parts reported that the tariffs 
  1960  will make the company's U.S. subsidiary its most expensive production 
  1961  facility. A commenter seeking an exemption for powersports vehicles 
  1962  reported that it relies on certain imported inputs and that a portion 
  1963  of its domestic manufacturing is supported by exports. Similarly, a 
  1964  comment regarding loudspeakers noted that domestic producers that rely 
  1965  on imported components are disadvantaged when selling in international 
  1966  markets when those components are subject to increased tariffs.
  1967      Products unrelated to the acts, policies, and practices 
  1968  investigated. Many comments argued that the tariffs should be narrowly 
  1969  tailored to specific products linked to forced labor. These comments 
  1970  noted that the products for which they requested exemption from tariffs 
  1971  were not related to the acts, policies, and practices found actionable 
  1972  in these investigations. Those products include: historical coins; 
  1973  radiators and other parts and accessories for motor vehicles; manuka 
  1974  honey; artificial floral, greenery, and seasonal decorative products; 
  1975  various electrical and lighting products; canned olives; and purified 
  1976  isophthalic acid. The comments emphasized that certain imports and 
  1977  sectors have no connection to forced labor. For example, regarding 
  1978  historical coins, a comment noted that the importation of those goods 
  1979  has no connection to forced labor because they were typically produced 
  1980  by skilled laborers or long ago.
  1981      Tariffs would not shift production to the United States. Some 
  1982  comments, such as those related to hydraulic log splitters, women's 
  1983  outerwear and insulated garments, stainless steel insulated drinkware, 
  1984  outer shell covers for pets, cyanate ester resins, crayons, salmon, and 
  1985  finished bovine upholstery leather argued that tariffs should not be 
  1986  applied to their products, as the tariffs would not shift production to 
  1987  the United States. Many of these comments argued that for a variety of 
  1988  reasons, production in the United States is not feasible.
  1989      Tariffs would cause economy-wide disruptions. Some comments, such 
  1990  as those related to toys and DL-methionine, suggested that tariffs 
  1991  would cause economy-wide disruptions. With respect to DL-methionine, 
  1992  commenters noted that tariffs risk serious disruption to the U.S. 
  1993  economy, including U.S. poultry, dairy, beef, and swine producers that 
  1994  depend on imports of that essential nutrient for livestock, and that 
  1995  the additional tariff is likely to disrupt the feed supply chain for 
  1996  U.S. livestock producers.
  1997      The President has directed the Trade Representative to impose 
  1998  tariffs on all goods of the 60 investigated economies, with certain 
  1999  exemptions. Exemptions directed by the President are limited to: (1) 
  2000  raw materials that if subject to the proposed additional tariffs could 
  2001  lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; (2) products that could 
  2002  cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to the proposed additional 
  2003  tariffs; (3) products that cannot be grown or produced in sufficient 
  2004  quantities or at reasonable prices in the United States or obtained 
  2005  from other sources; (4) products for which tariffs may not contribute 
  2006  substantially to the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices 
  2007  found to be actionable; or (5) products that if exempted from these 
  2008  tariffs would encourage economies that have made commitments to the 
  2009  United States regarding forced labor import prohibitions to implement 
  2010  those commitments or to enact and effectively enforce a forced labor 
  2011  import prohibition.
  2012      Considering the public comments and the advice of the Section 301 
  2013  Committee, as well as the advice of advisory committees--and in 
  2014  accordance with the specific direction of the President--the Trade 
  2015  Representative has determined that the goods above and other goods do 
  2016  not warrant exemption. With respect to the large number of the comments 
  2017  requesting exemption based on availability, most were not raw 
  2018  materials. Rather, most requests were for inputs or consumer goods. 
  2019  While some inputs and consumer goods may have limited or no 
  2020  availability from U.S. sources, those products should remain generally 
  2021  available and will not cause economy-wide disruptions if subjected to 
  2022  additional tariffs. Regarding tariffs resulting in increased costs, it 
  2023  is possible that costs will increase, but a number of factors may 
  2024  affect costs, and increased costs for a particular company or in a 
  2025  particular sector are unlikely to cause economy-wide disruptions. With 
  2026  respect to the argument that tariffs may result in a competitive 
  2027  disadvantage to certain domestic producers, a competitive disadvantage 
  2028  does not indicate unavailability of domestic supply or that products 
  2029  cannot be produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in 
  2030  the United States. Moreover, many inputs, including auto parts already 
  2031  subject to Section 232 tariffs, are exempt from additional tariffs 
  2032  pursuant to this action.
  2033      With respect to the comments that argued that the tariffs should be

**Reviewing annex clauses**

   341  United States during a certain period of time.
   342  
   343  V. Response to Significant Comments
   344  
   345      USTR responds below to significant issues raised in the public 
   346  comments and hearings in response to the March 17, 2026, Federal 
   347  Register notice.
   348  
   349  Response to Significant Comments Raising Legal Arguments Regarding 
   350  Findings of ``Unreasonableness''
   351  
   352      Multiple comments raised threshold arguments that the Trade 
   353  Representative should not find that the failure of an economy to impose 
   354  and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods 
   355  produced with forced labor is unreasonable where: (1) an economy has 
   356  domestic laws prohibiting forced labor; (2) where no international 
   357  standards exists which provide an affirmative obligation on economies 
   358  to impose a forced labor import prohibition; or (3) where an economy 
   359  has otherwise made commitments to the United States with respect to 
   360  imposing and/or enforcing a forced labor import prohibition. This 
   361  section takes each of these arguments in turn.
   362      With respect to the first argument, and as explained in the Report 
   363  and above, solely prohibiting forced labor domestically is unreasonable 
   364  because it fails to discipline the influx of forced labor goods or to 
   365  prevent domestic producers from using forced labor inputs. Thus, while 
   366  an economy may have taken steps to ensure that the condition of forced 
   367  labor is extinguished within its borders, the economy nevertheless 
   368  permits market conditions where imported forced labor goods have a 
   369  competitive advantage over U.S. goods imported into their economy.
   370      In response to the second argument, USTR notes the Section 301 
   371  statute,
   372  
   373  [[Page 34275]]
   374  
   375  which governs these investigations, does not require the existence of 
   376  international standards discipling specific conduct as a prerequisite 
   377  to a finding of an unreasonable act, policy, or practice under Section 
   378  301(b) of the Trade Act. As explained in the Report, the definition of 
   379  unreasonable acts, policies, and practices in Section 301(d) 
   380  contemplates circumstances where, as here, acts, policies, and 
   381  practices of a foreign country may not be inconsistent with or violate 
   382  the international legal rights of the United States, but are 
   383  nevertheless unfair. Thus, the statutory structure of Section 301 
   384  contemplates that the Trade Representative may find unreasonable 
   385  conduct on the part of a trading partner even in the absence of 
   386  international standards or obligations.
   387      Third, some comments argued that where an economy has made 
   388  commitments to the United States regarding forced labor import 
   389  prohibitions, including through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, the 
   390  Trade Representative is without basis to find that same economy's 
   391  failure to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import 
   392  prohibition is unreasonable. USTR applauds Argentina, Bangladesh, 
   393  Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia, and 
   394  Taiwan, which have undertaken commitments regarding a forced labor 
   395  import prohibition. However, commitments to take action in the future 
   396  is distinct from forbidding legally the importation of forced labor 
   397  goods, and effectively enforcing such prohibition. Until such time as 
   398  the commitment is implemented, U.S. products will continue to compete 
   399  against forced labor products that have a competitive advantage in 
   400  global markets which, among other reasons explained in the Report, is 
   401  unreasonable.
   402      The Trade Representative fully expects economies that have 
   403  undertaken commitments related to prohibiting the importation of forced 
   404  labor goods to abide by those commitments. Accordingly, the Trade 
   405  Representative proposes that the additional duty rate to be applied in 
   406  the investigations take into account whether an economy has undertaken 
   407  such commitments.
   408  
   409  Response to Significant Comments Regarding Actions To Be Taken in the 
   410  Investigations
   411  
   412      A number of comments responded on potential responsive action by 
   413  the Trade Representative. These comments recommended that the Trade 
   414  Representative engage in multilateral negotiations, including at the 
   415  ILO, to encourage economies to impose a forced labor import prohibition 
   416  rather than take ``punitive measures,'' and to provide capacity 
   417  building and technical assistance, especially to developing economies, 
   418  to encourage effective enforcement of such a prohibition.
   419      The Trade Representative proposes that taking an action is 
   420  appropriate, and that action includes the imposition of additional 
   421  duties on products of the investigated economies, in order to obtain 
   422  the elimination of the investigated acts, policies, or practices. 
   423  However, the Trade Representative will continue to consider these 
   424  comments in conjunction with any action that might be taken with 
   425  respect to the investigations.

**Reviewing tariff notes**

I’m narrowing the memo to the operative tariff provisions and the specific exceptions needed for Q12, Q9, Q13, and Q15. I’m checking the relevant annex notes, headings, and footnotes, including USMCA treatment for Mexico and Canada, Section 232 exceptions, and Section 301 provisions. The key goal is to distinguish original proposals from enacted language and identify the precise subheadings governing each exception.**Applying Dominican exceptions**

I’m working through Q8’s timing scenarios using the Dominican rate and the stated transit cutoff. Goods loaded before the deadline may qualify only when they remain in transit on the required final mode; air cargo does not fit that vessel-specific exception. Entries before the effective date avoid the tariff, while bonded goods withdrawn afterward generally remain subject to it. I’m also checking the pharmaceutical exception, especially the relevant tariff heading and whether patented pharmaceutical articles are excluded or covered under the specified effective-date language.

summary.text:
**Clarifying effective dates**

I’m organizing the Section 338 timeline by document, publication date, and operative date. The initial proclamation was signed July 23 and published July 20, while the later suspension applied to entries or warehouse withdrawals beginning August 22. September changes generally applied from September 15, with certain exclusions effective upon importation on September 29. The October scope changes applied to entries or withdrawals from October 30. For alcoholic beverages, I’m tracking the initial imposition, delay, exclusions, and subsequent scope modifications, with no later changes noted.**Tracking product changes**

I’m mapping each product group against its imposition, delay, exclusion, and later scope changes. Dairy follows imposition, delay, and a September 29 exclusion, with no additional scope modification identified. Motor vehicles have a more complex sequence: initial imposition, delay, September exclusions and revisions, then an October 30 reversal affecting which products remain covered. For individual products, P remains covered after September 15, Q leaves coverage then, R remains covered until October 30, and S becomes covered on October 30.

**Evaluating duty timing**

I’m organizing the applicable provisions by entry date: September 14, September 15, October 29 at 4 p.m., October 30 at 12:01 a.m., and November 3. The key changes occur when the duty becomes effective and when the text changes regarding overlap with Section 232. Initially, Section 338 does not apply to Section 232 articles, but the September and October language makes it additional to Section 232. I’m also checking whether the products remain in Annex II and whether any dairy exclusion affects the result.**Applying alcohol timing**

I’m distinguishing arrival dates from consumption-entry or warehouse-withdrawal dates. Shipment A arrived September 10 and entered September 14, before the September 15 scope change and before the September 29 import ban, so I’m treating it as permitted with a 50% duty, totaling $15,000. Shipment B arrived September 27 but was withdrawn October 5; because it entered before the ban, I’m treating the withdrawal as permitted while retaining the 50% duty, also $15,000. Shipment C’s timing is incomplete, so I’m continuing from its arrival time.

**Analyzing entry dates**

I'm distinguishing between arrival, importation, entry, and later withdrawal from a foreign-trade zone. Goods arriving before September 29 appear allowed, though those not entered beforehand may still incur the 50% duty; that would put the assessed amount at $15,000 for the September 28 shipment.

The September 29, 12:30 a.m. shipment appears barred from importation, so the exclusion likely overrides ordinary duty treatment. The foreign-trade-zone goods are less certain: admission before September 29 may not equal importation, while the October 6 withdrawal could trigger the relevant restriction or duty.**Resolving FTZ treatment**

I'm reading the language as focusing on when the goods were imported or admitted, not merely when they were later withdrawn. Because the FTZ goods arrived on September 25, before the September 29 restriction, they likely aren't excluded from importation. However, their admission after the earlier effective date may require privileged foreign status, making the 50% duty payable when withdrawn for consumption on October 6—apparently $15,000. If the later exclusion is invalidated, the specified fallback duty would apply instead.

**Interpreting tariff changes**

I’m distinguishing between products covered by the scope modification and goods remaining subject to the original tariff. The exclusion for alcohol appears to leave the underlying 50% duty intact where the product is outside the modified scope, while the modification itself continues governing affected products.

For the timing calculation, I’m applying the amended rate only after its effective moment: the first two entries, before August 22, owe $0, while the third owes 50% of $40,000, or $20,000. Any earlier deposits would be handled through the applicable refund process.**Clarifying effective dates**

I’m treating the August 22 start date as controlling: an earlier entry may have been deposited despite no duty being effective, but the documents do not appear to promise an automatic refund. Instead, any refund would follow the applicable customs procedures where required.

I’m also concluding that no later presidential action was necessary. The original measure established the effective date, and the suspension simply lapsed after the stated conditions were unmet. For the separate 30-day calculation, July 20 plus 30 days lands on August 19.

**Clarifying the effective date**

I’m distinguishing the proclamation’s signing date from its publication date. The text says the suspension starts no earlier than 30 days after the President’s proclamation finding. Counting from the signing date, July 20 plus 30 days reaches August 19: July 21 is day one, and August 19 is day 30. Counting from publication on July 23 would instead reach August 22. That difference matters because the revised date appears to align with publication-based counting, creating the discrepancy addressed in the later question.**Comparing effective dates**

I’m separating the original duty from later scope changes. The October document was signed October 23, filed October 29, published October 30, and applied to entries or withdrawals occurring on or after 12:01 a.m. October 30. It therefore operated prospectively, without providing refunds for earlier entries. The original duty began August 22, while later additions became effective seven days after signing: September 15 for P and October 30 for S. The documents do not expressly reconcile those shorter periods with the 30-day baseline.

**Assessing Liechtenstein’s treatment**

I’m checking whether Liechtenstein appears among the 60 economies covered by the Section 301 investigation. The list includes Switzerland but not Liechtenstein, so the available text does not establish that Liechtenstein is treated as Switzerland for this purpose.

Because the product is identified as originating in Liechtenstein, I’m leaning toward no additional Section 301 duty, while noting that the customs union alone may not determine tariff treatment. Hong Kong and India appear separately at 12.5% and 10%, respectively.**Clarifying Liechtenstein’s duty**

I’m explicitly flagging the conclusion: under the notice being analyzed, Liechtenstein is not one of the 60 listed economies, so this action does not impose a Section 301 duty on Liechtenstein-origin products. I’m treating that as distinct from any possible customs relationship with Switzerland, which the notice itself may not address. If the applicable MFN duty is 4,000, the total remains 4,000 because no additional Section 301 amount is imposed under this action.

**Comparing tariff categories**

I’m calculating the implied rates for the listed economies under the stated MFN thresholds and comparing them with the June proposal.

Germany and the EU receive 0%, Japan 0.5%, Taiwan 0%, South Korea 2.5%, and Switzerland 12.5% under the assumptions provided. I’m also distinguishing the June proposal from later enacted measures, since the final 10% list expanded to include additional economies. Honduras appears to require special treatment because it was not clearly included in the original proposal categories.**Distinguishing rate treatment**

I’m separating the numerical rates from how they’re calculated. Switzerland and Norway remain at 12.5%, while the UK remains at 10%. Germany and the EU may shift from a proposed flat 10% to a final rate calculated net of MFN duties, subject to a cap. Taiwan’s number remains 10%, but its treatment changes similarly. Japan’s final 12.5% may be net of MFN rather than a flat rate. Liechtenstein has no identified rate. India falls from a proposed 12.5% to 10%.

**Checking tariff comparisons**

I’m comparing the proposed notice with the later action, focusing on economy categories, MFN calculations, exemptions, and changed rates. The likely differences involve Switzerland, the EU, Taiwan, Japan, and India, while Liechtenstein may have no separate action.

For France, treated under the EU category, the MFN duty is 3 cents per kilogram. At 2,000 kilograms, that equals $60, or 0.5% of a $12,000 customs value. To reach a 10% total duty, the additional duty would be 9.5%, totaling $1,140.**Calculating equivalent duties**

I’m applying the rule that converts MFN duties into an ad valorem equivalent by dividing payable MFN duty by customs value. For Italy, the combined MFN amount is $1,800 on $20,000, or 9%; the additional duty to reach 10% is $200. Japan requires 3.5%, or $700, to reach 12.5%. Brazil’s flat 12.5% produces $2,500 without subtracting MFN.

For Taiwan, an 11% MFN equivalent exceeds the 10% target, so additional duty is zero. Switzerland is 1.5% below its 12.5% cap, producing $300.

**Determining applicable duties**

I’m applying the dates and exceptions item by item. Entries before July 24 appear exempt, while goods entering or withdrawn afterward generally face the 10% duty.

The transit exception requires loading before July 24, so goods loaded July 24 or later don’t qualify. It also appears limited to vessel shipments, excluding the July 23 air shipment.

I’m distinguishing the presidential memorandum’s July 23 signature from the duty’s July 24, 12:01 a.m. applicability and the notice’s July 28 publication. The pharmaceutical article entering July 30 receives the 12.5% rate.**Applying tariff exceptions**

I’m treating the August 3 pharmaceutical entry as exempt because the addendum became effective July 31 and specifically excludes the relevant patented-pharmaceutical headings. The product may therefore remain subject only to its ordinary tariff treatment.

For the Thailand assembly, I’m excluding the $35,000 value of U.S.-made components from the $100,000 article, leaving $65,000 subject to the 12.5% rate, or $8,125.

For the repaired U.S. machine returned from Israel, I’m applying the 12.5% rate only to the $6,000 repair value, producing $750.

**Verifying tariff treatment**

I’m checking the Mexico classification first. The key issue is whether the goods qualify for USMCA treatment under the relevant U.S. note and whether the special Chapter 99 heading is exempt. If USMCA applies, the duty would be 0%; otherwise, a 10% rate on $50,000 would produce $5,000.

I’m also reviewing the Japanese passenger-car entry under heading 9903.94.01, focusing on whether the Section 301 note expressly includes or excludes vehicles classified under the listed Section 232 headings.

summary.text:
**Clarifying tariff treatment**

I’m distinguishing the specific exclusions from broader proposed exemptions. For Q9(d), I’m reading no Section 301 duty because the product falls within the explicitly covered F2 category, producing $0.

For Q9(e), Brazil’s 12.5% rate appears to remain applicable. The Section 232 treatment is tied to specifically listed headings, not a general exemption, so the calculation is $12,500.

For Q9(f), I’m treating the June proposal’s broad exemptions for Section 232 articles, informational materials, and donations as removed or narrowed in the adopted text.**Calculating scenario ten**

I’m treating the adopted text as controlling: it applies broadly except for specifically listed annex categories, so informational materials, donations, and Section 232 goods do not receive a separate blanket exemption.

For the Canadian aluminum extrusions, I’m calculating 3% MFN duty ($6,000), 50% Section 232 duty ($100,000), and no Section 338 or Section 301 duty because the product falls within the relevant Section 232 exclusion. summary.text:
**Reviewing tariff changes**

I’m checking a February 20, 2026 executive order that may end tariff actions imposed under IEEPA, while separating those measures from any existing import surcharge. I’m also comparing related documents, including the orders numbered 2026-03832 and 2026-03824, along with the 2025 Canada-related materials. The key distinction is whether reciprocal tariffs are ending while a temporary surcharge under Section 122 continues. I need to verify the order’s exact language and effective date before drawing a firm conclusion.

    65                  Proclamation 11012 of February 20, 2026
    66  
    67                  
    68  Imposing a Temporary Import Surcharge To Address 
    69                  Fundamental International Payments Problems
    70  
    71                  By the President of the United States of America
    72  
    73                  A Proclamation
    74  
    75                  1. The United States plays a pivotal role in shaping 
    76                  the global economy. At the same time, the United States 
    77                  faces various threats to its own economy and national 
    78                  interests. Sometimes, the United States faces 
    79                  fundamental international payments problems, such as 
    80                  large and serious balance-of-payments deficits, an 
    81                  imminent and significant depreciation of its currency 
    82                  in foreign exchange markets, or an international 
    83                  balance-of-payments disequilibrium. These problems can, 
    84                  among other things, endanger the ability of the United 
    85                  States to finance its spending, erode investor 
    86                  confidence in the economy, and distress the financial 
    87                  markets.
    88  
    89                  2. Special import measures to restrict imports, such as 
    90                  surcharges and quotas, are key tools to protect the 
    91                  economy and national security of the United States, 
    92                  and, in certain circumstances, they are required to 
    93                  deal with fundamental international payments problems.
    94  
    95                  3. Given the gravity of fundamental international 
    96                  payments problems and the importance of import 
    97                  restrictions as economic, national security, and 
    98                  foreign policy tools, Federal law, including section 
    99                  122 of the Trade Act of 1974 (19 U.S.C. 2132) (section 
   100                  122), empowers the President to take action through 
   101                  surcharges and other special import restrictions to 
   102                  address fundamental international payments problems.
   103  
   104                  4. I have received certain requested information and 
   105                  opinions from senior officials on whether any 
   106                  fundamental international payments problems exist and 
   107                  the extent to which such problems could impair United 
   108                  States national interests, including economic and 
   109                  national security interests. The information and 
   110                  opinions discuss, among other things, the state of the 
   111                  balance of payments of the United States, the standing 
   112                  of the United States dollar in foreign exchange 
   113                  markets, and the state of international balances of 
   114                  payments. I have also received opinions and 
   115                  recommendations from senior officials on whether 
   116                  special import measures to restrict imports are 
   117                  required to address any fundamental international 
   118                  payments problems. These opinions address, among other 
   119                  things, whether a surcharge in the form of ad valorem 
   120                  duties is required to restrict imports to deal with 
   121                  large and serious United States balance-of-payments 
   122                  deficits, to prevent an imminent and significant 
   123                  depreciation of the United States dollar in foreign 
   124                  exchange markets, or to cooperate with other countries 
   125                  in correcting an international balance-of-payments 
   126                  disequilibrium.
   127  
   128                  5. These senior officials have informed me that 
   129                  fundamental international payments problems within the 
   130                  meaning of section 122 exist and that special import 
   131                  measures to restrict imports are required to address 
   132                  these problems. Specifically, my advisors have 
   133                  determined that an import surcharge in the form of ad 
   134                  valorem duties is required to deal with large and 
   135                  serious United States balance-of-payments deficits. My 
   136                  advisors have also opined that certain products should 
   137                  not be subject to the surcharge because of the needs of 
   138                  the United States economy and that the recommended 
   139                  exceptions are consistent with the limitations of 
   140                  section 122, the purposes of section 122, and the 
   141                  national interest of the United States.
   142  
   143  [[Page 9340]]
   144  
   145                  6. Among other things, I have been informed by my 
   146                  advisors that the United States balance-of-payments 
   147                  position, under any reasonable understanding of the 
   148                  term in the context of section 122, is currently a 
   149                  large and serious deficit. My advisors have studied 
   150                  different methods of evaluating balance-of-payments 
   151                  deficits, including calculations based on current-
   152                  account statistics. In my advisors' opinions, under any 
   153                  of these methods, the United States balance-of-payments 
   154                  position is a large and serious deficit.
   155  
   156                  7. For instance, my advisors have informed me that the 
   157                  United States runs a deficit in selling goods and 
   158                  services overseas, as reported by the United States 
   159                  Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in the ``balance on 
   160                  goods and services''; has recently reflected quarterly 
   161                  deficits in its return on investment or labor, as 
   162                  reported by the BEA in the ``balance on primary 
   163                  income''; and runs a deficit in voluntary transfers, 
   164                  such as remittances, as reported by the BEA in the 
   165                  ``balance on secondary income.'' In other words, the 
   166                  United States runs a trade deficit, does not currently 
   167                  make a net income from the capital and labor that it 
   168                  deploys abroad, and experiences more transfer payments, 
   169                  on net, flowing out of the country than into the 
   170                  country.
   171  
   172                  8. As my advisors have informed me, the United States 
   173                  runs a substantial trade deficit. The large, 
   174                  persistent, and serious annual United States goods 
   175                  trade deficit has grown by over 40 percent in the past 
   176                  5 years alone, reaching $1.2 trillion in 2024. In 2025, 
   177                  the United States goods trade deficit remained at 
   178                  approximately $1.2 trillion. The effects of this 
   179                  deficit are serious, and this deficit contributes to 
   180                  the fundamental international payments problems facing 
   181                  the United States.
   182  
   183                  9. As my advisors have also informed me, the annual 
   184                  balance on the United States primary income turned 
   185                  negative for the first time since at least 1960 in 
   186                  2024. From 1960 to 2023, the United States ran a 
   187                  surplus in its annual balance on primary income. That 
   188                  positive balance on primary income served as a 
   189                  stabilizing force for the United States balance-of-
   190                  payments position even in the face of large and 
   191                  persistent trade deficits. In 2024, however, the 
   192                  balance on primary income turned negative and thus 
   193                  ceased to serve as a counterweight to the trade deficit 
   194                  in the United States current account. Indeed, in 2024, 
   195                  the United States maintained a current account deficit 
   196                  of 4.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), almost 
   197                  double the current account deficit of approximately 2.0 
   198                  percent that prevailed between 2013 and 2019, and 
   199                  larger than that which prevailed from 2019 to 2023. As 
   200                  a share of GDP, the staggering deficit of 4.0 percent 
   201                  represented the biggest annual current account deficit 
   202                  since 2008.
   203  
   204                  10. As my advisors have also informed me, the net 
   205                  international-investment position of the United States 
   206                  is in an ongoing decline. According to the BEA, at the 
   207                  end of 2024, the net international-investment position 
   208                  of the United States, as a share of GDP, was negative 
   209                  90 percent, a sharp deterioration from the average of 
   210                  negative 41 percent in the decade between 2010 and 
   211                  2020. In my advisors' view, this is a highly atypical 
   212                  position for a country, particularly the United States. 
   213                  Indeed, both in terms of United States dollars and as a 
   214                  share of GDP, this represents one of the most negative 
   215                  net international-investment positions of any developed 
   216                  country. Because the current account is one of the 
   217                  primary drivers of changes in the net international-
   218                  investment position, the atypically large negative net 
   219                  international-investment position of the United States 
   220                  shows that the United States balance-of-payments 
   221                  deficit is large and serious.
   222  
   223                  11. Further, as my advisors have informed me, the 
   224                  balance on secondary income of the United States has 
   225                  been persistently in a deficit since the 1960s.
   226  
   227                  12. According to my advisors, an import surcharge in 
   228                  the form of ad valorem duties is required to address 
   229                  these fundamental international payments problems. In 
   230                  my advisors' opinions, imposing an import surcharge 
   231                  would deal with the large and serious United States 
   232                  balance-of-payments deficit. My advisors have further 
   233                  recommended that certain products should not be subject 
   234                  to the surcharge because of the needs of the United 
   235                  States economy
   236  
   237  [[Page 9341]]
   238  
   239                  and have opined that a surcharge with certain 
   240                  exceptions would more effectively deal with the 
   241                  balance-of-payments deficit than would a surcharge 
   242                  without the exceptions.
   243  
   244                  13. After considering the information, opinions, and 
   245                  recommendations that have been provided to me by senior 
   246                  officials, among other relevant information and 
   247                  considerations, I find that fundamental international 
   248                  payments problems within the meaning of section 122 
   249                  exist; that those problems significantly harm United 
   250                  States national interests, including economic and 
   251                  national security interests; and that special measures 
   252                  to restrict imports are required to address those 
   253                  problems, as authorized by section 122. Specifically, I 
   254                  find that a surcharge in the form of ad valorem duties 
   255                  on certain imports is required to deal with the United 
   256                  States' large and serious balance-of-payments deficit. 
   257                  Accordingly, I impose, for a period of 150 days, a 
   258                  temporary import surcharge of 10 percent ad valorem, as 
   259                  described below, on articles imported into the United 
   260                  States, effective February 24, 2026.

    28  
    29                  
    30  Imposing Duties To Address the Flow of Illicit 
    31                  Drugs Across Our Northern Border
    32  
    33                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    34                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    35                  America, including the International Emergency Economic 
    36                  Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) (IEEPA), the 
    37                  National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.) 
    38                  (NEA), section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended 
    39                  (19 U.S.C. 2483), and section 301 of title 3, United 
    40                  States Code,
    41  
    42                  I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of 
    43                  America, find that the sustained influx of illicit 
    44                  opioids and other drugs has profound consequences on 
    45                  our Nation, endangering lives and putting a severe 
    46                  strain on our healthcare system, public services, and 
    47                  communities.
    48  
    49                  This challenge threatens the fabric of our society. 
    50                  Gang members, smugglers, human traffickers, and illicit 
    51                  drugs of all kinds have poured across our borders and 
    52                  into our communities. Canada has played a central role 
    53                  in these challenges, including by failing to devote 
    54                  sufficient attention and resources or meaningfully 
    55                  coordinate with United States law enforcement partners 
    56                  to effectively stem the tide of illicit drugs.
    57  
    58                  Drug trafficking organizations (DTOs) are the world's 
    59                  leading producers of fentanyl, methamphetamine, 
    60                  cocaine, and other illicit drugs, and they cultivate, 
    61                  process, and distribute massive quantities of narcotics 
    62                  that fuel addiction and violence in communities across 
    63                  the United States. These DTOs often collaborate with 
    64                  transnational cartels to smuggle illicit drugs into the 
    65                  United States, utilizing clandestine airstrips, 
    66                  maritime routes, and overland corridors.
    67  
    68                  The challenges at our southern border are foremost in 
    69                  the public consciousness, but our northern border is 
    70                  not exempt from these issues. Criminal networks are 
    71                  implicated in human trafficking and smuggling 
    72                  operations, enabling unvetted illegal migration across 
    73                  our northern border. There is also a growing presence 
    74                  of Mexican cartels operating fentanyl and nitazene 
    75                  synthesis labs in Canada. The flow of illicit drugs 
    76                  like fentanyl to the United States through both illicit 
    77                  distribution networks and international mail--due, in 
    78                  the case of the latter, to the existing administrative 
    79                  exemption from duty and taxes, also known as de 
    80                  minimis, under section 1321 of title 19, United States 
    81                  Code--has created a public health crisis in the United 
    82                  States, as outlined in the Presidential Memorandum of 
    83                  January 20, 2025 (America First Trade Policy) and 
    84                  Executive Order 14157 of January 20, 2025 (Designating 
    85                  Cartels and Other Organizations as Foreign Terrorist 
    86                  Organizations and Specially Designated Global 
    87                  Terrorists). With respect to smuggling of illicit drugs 
    88                  across our northern border, Canada's Financial 
    89                  Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre recently 
    90                  published a study on the laundering of proceeds of 
    91                  illicit synthetic opioids, which recognized Canada's 
    92                  heightened domestic production of fentanyl, largely 
    93                  from British Columbia, and its growing footprint within 
    94                  international narcotics distribution. Despite a North 
    95                  American dialogue on the public health impacts of 
    96                  illicit drugs since 2016, Canadian officials have 
    97                  acknowledged that the problem has only grown. And while 
    98                  U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) within the

    60                  extraordinary threat beyond our northern border.

    59                  
    60  Regulating Imports With a Reciprocal Tariff To 
    61                  Rectify Trade Practices That Contribute to Large and 
    62                  Persistent Annual United States Goods Trade Deficits
    63  
    64                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    65                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    66                  America, including the International Emergency Economic 
    67                  Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.)(IEEPA), the 
    68                  National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.)(NEA), 
    69                  section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
    70                  U.S.C. 2483), and section 301 of title 3, United States 
    71                  Code,
    72  
    73                  I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of 
    74                  America, find that underlying conditions, including a 
    75                  lack of reciprocity in our bilateral trade 
    76                  relationships, disparate tariff rates and non-tariff 
    77                  barriers, and U.S. trading partners' economic policies 
    78                  that suppress domestic wages and consumption, as 
    79                  indicated by large and persistent annual U.S. goods 
    80                  trade deficits, constitute an unusual and extraordinary 
    81                  threat to the national security and economy of the 
    82                  United States. That threat has its source in whole or 
    83                  substantial part outside the United States in the 
    84                  domestic economic policies of key trading partners and 
    85                  structural imbalances in the global trading system. I 
    86                  hereby declare a national emergency with respect to 
    87                  this threat.
    88  
    89                  On January 20, 2025, I signed the America First Trade 
    90                  Policy Presidential Memorandum directing my 
    91                  Administration to investigate the causes of our 
    92                  country's large and persistent annual trade deficits in 
    93                  goods, including the economic and national security 
    94                  implications and risks resulting from such deficits, 
    95                  and to undertake a review of, and identify, any unfair 
    96                  trade practices by other countries. On February 13, 
    97                  2025, I signed a Presidential Memorandum entitled 
    98                  ``Reciprocal Trade and Tariffs,'' that directed further 
    99                  review of our trading partners' non-reciprocal trading 
   100                  practices, and noted the relationship between non-
   101                  reciprocal practices and the trade deficit. On April 1, 
   102                  2025, I received the final results of those 
   103                  investigations, and I am taking action today based on 
   104                  those results.
   105  
   106                  Large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits 
   107                  have led to the hollowing out of our manufacturing 
   108                  base; inhibited our ability to scale advanced domestic 
   109                  manufacturing capacity; undermined critical supply 
   110                  chains; and rendered our defense-industrial base 
   111                  dependent on foreign adversaries. Large and persistent 
   112                  annual U.S. goods trade deficits are caused in 
   113                  substantial part by a lack of reciprocity in our 
   114                  bilateral trade relationships. This situation is 
   115                  evidenced by disparate tariff rates and non-tariff 
   116                  barriers that make it harder for U.S. manufacturers to 
   117                  sell their products in foreign markets. It is also 
   118                  evidenced by the economic policies of key U.S. trading 
   119                  partners insofar as they suppress domestic wages and 
   120                  consumption, and thereby demand for U.S. exports, while 
   121                  artificially increasing the competitiveness of their 
   122                  goods in global markets. These conditions have given 
   123                  rise to the national emergency that this order is 
   124                  intended to abate and resolve.
   125  
   126                  For decades starting in 1934, U.S. trade policy has 
   127                  been organized around the principle of reciprocity. The 
   128                  Congress directed the President to secure reduced 
   129                  reciprocal tariff rates from key trading partners first 
   130                  through bilateral trade agreements and later under the 
   131                  auspices of the global trading system. Between 1934 and 
   132                  1945, the executive branch negotiated and signed 32 
   133                  bilateral reciprocal trade agreements designed to lower 
   134                  tariff rates on a
   135  
   136  [[Page 15042]]
   137  
   138                  reciprocal basis. After 1947 through 1994, 
   139                  participating countries engaged in eight rounds of 
   140                  negotiation, which resulted in the General Agreements 
   141                  on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and seven subsequent tariff 
   142                  reduction rounds.
   143  
   144                  However, despite a commitment to the principle of 
   145                  reciprocity, the trading relationship between the 
   146                  United States and its trading partners has become 
   147                  highly unbalanced, particularly in recent years. The 
   148                  post-war international economic system was based upon 
   149                  three incorrect assumptions: first, that if the United 
   150                  States led the world in liberalizing tariff and non-
   151                  tariff barriers the rest of the world would follow; 
   152                  second, that such liberalization would ultimately 
   153                  result in more economic convergence and increased 
   154                  domestic consumption among U.S. trading partners 
   155                  converging towards the share in the United States; and 
   156                  third, that as a result, the United States would not 
   157                  accrue large and persistent goods trade deficits.
   158  
   159                  This framework set in motion events, agreements, and 
   160                  commitments that did not result in reciprocity or 
   161                  generally increase domestic consumption in foreign 
   162                  economies relative to domestic consumption in the 
   163                  United States. Those events, in turn, created large and 
   164                  persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits as a 
   165                  feature of the global trading system.
   166  
   167                  Put simply, while World Trade Organization (WTO) 
   168                  Members agreed to bind their tariff rates on a most-
   169                  favored-nation (MFN) basis, and thereby provide their 
   170                  best tariff rates to all WTO Members, they did not 
   171                  agree to bind their tariff rates at similarly low 
   172                  levels or to apply tariff rates on a reciprocal basis. 
   173                  Consequently, according to the WTO, the United States 
   174                  has among the lowest simple average MFN tariff rates in 
   175                  the world at 3.3 percent, while many of our key trading 
   176                  partners like Brazil (11.2 percent), China (7.5 
   177                  percent), the European Union (EU) (5 percent), India 
   178                  (17 percent), and Vietnam (9.4 percent) have simple 
   179                  average MFN tariff rates that are significantly higher.
   180  
   181                  Moreover, these average MFN tariff rates conceal much 
   182                  larger discrepancies across economies in tariff rates 
   183                  applied to particular products. For example, the United 
   184                  States imposes a 2.5 percent tariff on passenger 
   185                  vehicle imports (with internal combustion engines), 
   186                  while the European Union (10 percent), India (70 
   187                  percent), and China (15 percent) impose much higher 
   188                  duties on the same product. For network switches and 
   189                  routers, the United States imposes a 0 percent tariff, 
   190                  but for similar products, India (10 percent) levies a 
   191                  higher rate. Brazil (18 percent) and Indonesia (30 
   192                  percent) impose a higher tariff on ethanol than does 
   193                  the United States (2.5 percent). For rice in the husk, 
   194                  the U.S. MFN tariff is 2.7 percent (ad valorem 
   195                  equivalent), while India (80 percent), Malaysia (40 
   196                  percent), and Turkey (an average of 31 percent) impose 
   197                  higher rates. Apples enter the United States duty-free, 
   198                  but not so in Turkey (60.3 percent) and India (50 
   199                  percent).
   200  
   201                  Similarly, non-tariff barriers also deprive U.S. 
   202                  manufacturers of reciprocal access to markets around 
   203                  the world. The 2025 National Trade Estimate Report on 
   204                  Foreign Trade Barriers (NTE) details a great number of 
   205                  non-tariff barriers to U.S. exports around the world on 
   206                  a trading-partner by trading-partner basis. These 
   207                  barriers include import barriers and licensing

   219                  affecting trade in digital products; investment

summary.text:
**Clarifying tariff phases**

I’m mapping the remaining 2025 IEEPA amendments by effective date, but the timeline still has a few uncertainties. My current reading is that entries on February 10 faced no IEEPA tariff because the earlier pause remained in effect. The March 4 action introduced the 25% rate, while the March 6 amendment, effective March 7, exempted qualifying USMCA goods. Nonqualifying goods apparently remained at 25%. I’m still checking whether March 10 or March 14 introduced another transition or merely preserved that rate.**Tracking tariff treatment**

I’m distinguishing the general IEEPA rate from the separate aluminum Section 232 treatment. For a March 6 entry, I’m currently reading the 25% IEEPA tariff as applying to both N and U because the USMCA exemption did not become effective until March 7. On March 10 and March 14, N would remain at 25%, while qualifying U goods would be zero-rated under IEEPA. Aluminum may still carry its separate Section 232 duty. Later 2025 changes require separate date verification.

**Researching tariff timelines**

I’m checking how USMCA treatment interacts with the aluminum measures described here. The key issue is that Section 232 rates and coverage may have changed during 2025, including a possible increase to 50% in June, while the question also assumes a new heading beginning April 6, 2026.

I need to verify the relevant proclamations and amendments, then organize the applicable rates by period. I’m also checking whether the earlier 25% treatment applied to the full aluminum value before those later changes.
