    78                  section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as 
    79                  amended (19 U.S.C. 1862) (section 232). The Secretary 
    80                  found and advised me of the Secretary's opinion that 
    81                  aluminum is being imported into the United States in 
    82                  such quantities and under such circumstances as to 
    83                  threaten to impair the national security of the United 
    84                  States.
    85  
    86                  2. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    87                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), I 
    88                  concurred in the Secretary's finding that aluminum was 
    89                  being imported into the United States in such 
    90                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    91                  to impair the national security of the United States, 
    92                  and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum articles 
    93                  by imposing a 10 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    94                  articles imported from most countries. Proclamation 
    95                  9704 further stated that any country with which the 
    96                  United States has a security relationship is welcome to 
    97                  discuss alternative ways to address the threatened 
    98                  impairment of the national security caused by imports 
    99                  from that country, and noted that, should the United 
   100                  States and any such country arrive at a satisfactory 
   101                  alternative means to address the threat to the national 
   102                  security such that I determine that imports from that 
   103                  country no longer threaten to impair the national 
   104                  security, I may remove or modify the restriction on 
   105                  aluminum articles imports from that country and, if 
   106                  necessary, adjust the tariff as it applies to other 
   107                  countries, as the national security interests of the 
   108                  United States require.
   109  
   110                  3. In Proclamation 9704, I also directed the Secretary 
   111                  to monitor imports of aluminum articles and inform me 
   112                  of any circumstances that in the Secretary's opinion 
   113                  might indicate the need for further action under 
   114                  section 232 with respect to such imports. Pursuant to 
   115                  Proclamation 9704, the Secretary was authorized to 
   116                  provide relief from the additional duties, based on a 
   117                  request from a directly affected party located in the 
   118                  United States, for any aluminum article determined not 
   119                  to be produced in the United States in a sufficient and 
   120                  reasonably available amount or of a satisfactory 
   121                  quality, or based upon specific national security 
   122                  considerations. Proclamation 9776 of August 29, 2018, 
   123                  and Proclamation 9980 of January 24, 2020, similarly 
   124                  authorized the Secretary to provide relief from certain 
   125                  tariffs on other aluminum products and derivatives set 
   126                  forth in those proclamations.
   127  
   128                  4. In subsequent proclamations, the President adjusted 
   129                  the tariffs applicable to aluminum articles imports 
   130                  from Argentina, Australia, Canada, Mexico, the European 
   131                  Union (EU), and the United Kingdom (UK), after engaging 
   132                  in discussions with each of those parties on 
   133                  alternative ways to address the threat to the national 
   134                  security from such imports.
   135  
   136                  5. The Secretary has informed me that, notwithstanding 
   137                  the 10 percent ad valorem tariff imposed by 
   138                  Proclamation 9704 that mitigated the threatened 
   139                  impairment of our national security, aluminum imports 
   140                  into the United States have continued at unacceptable 
   141                  levels as the global aluminum excess capacity crisis 
   142                  continues. In addition, the exclusion of certain 
   143                  countries
   144  
   145  [[Page 9808]]
   146  
   147                  and products from the tariff and efforts by foreign 
   148                  producers to circumvent the tariff have undermined the 
   149                  purpose of Proclamation 9704, which was to adjust the 
   150                  level of imports of aluminum to remove the threatened 
   151                  impairment of the national security. This has again 
   152                  resulted in aluminum smelter capacity utilization rates 
   153                  in the domestic aluminum industry that are well below 
   154                  the target level recommended in the Secretary's January 
   155                  19, 2018, report. This indicates that the initial 
   156                  tariff of 10 percent ad valorem is not high enough to 
   157                  address the threatened impairment to our national 
   158                  security posed by aluminum imports.
   159  
   160                  6. In particular, the Secretary has informed me that 
   161                  global primary aluminum capacity has continued to 
   162                  increase, fueled by expansions in the People's Republic 
   163                  of China (China) and South America, which is seen in 
   164                  rising aluminum imports that continue to weigh on the 
   165                  price domestic aluminum producers may charge. There has 
   166                  also been a significant increase in Chinese investment 
   167                  in Mexico, driven by massive Chinese government 
   168                  subsidies and the continued ability to exploit 
   169                  loopholes in U.S. trade policy.
   170  
   171                  7. Domestic aluminum producers have been forced to idle 
   172                  additional production and shut down facilities. Two 
   173                  primary aluminum smelters within the United States have 
   174                  closed since Proclamation 9704 was promulgated. In 
   175                  addition, U.S. primary aluminum production decreased by 
   176                  30 percent from 2020 to 2024, and U.S. smelter capacity 
   177                  utilization was only 52 percent in 2024. Overcapacity 
   178                  for primary aluminum has harmed downstream aluminum 
   179                  producers, including producers of aluminum extrusions 
   180                  and aluminum sheet. To allow U.S. aluminum producers to

    33  
    34                  By the President of the United States of America

    36                  A Proclamation
    37  
    38                  1. On January 11, 2018, the Secretary of Commerce 
    39                  (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on the 
    40                  Secretary's investigation into the effect of imports of

    53                  Imports of Derivative Aluminum Articles and Derivative

    55                  with the Secretary's findings that steel articles, as

    58                  Proclamation 9980, are being imported into the United

    61                  United States, and I decided to adjust the imports of 
    62                  those steel articles and derivative steel articles by 
    63                  imposing a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    64                  articles imported from most countries. In Proclamation 
    65                  10896 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Steel 
    66                  Into the United States), I decided to adjust the 
    67                  imports of steel articles and derivative steel articles 
    68                  by imposing a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    69                  articles imported from all countries.
    70  
    71                  3. On January 19, 2018, the Secretary transmitted to me 
    72                  a report on the Secretary's investigation into the 
    73                  effect of imports of aluminum articles on the national 
    74                  security of the United States under section 232. The 
    75                  Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that 
    76                  aluminum articles are being imported into the United 
    77                  States in such quantities and under such circumstances 
    78                  as to threaten to impair the national security of the 
    79                  United States.
    80  
    81                  4. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    82                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), and 
    83                  Proclamation 9980, I concurred with the Secretary's 
    84                  findings that aluminum articles, as defined in clause 1 
    85                  of Proclamation 9704, and derivative aluminum articles, 
    86                  as described in clause 3 of Proclamation 9980, are 
    87                  being imported into the United States in such 
    88                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    89                  to impair the national security of the United States, 
    90                  and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum articles 
    91                  and derivative aluminum articles by imposing a 10 
    92                  percent ad valorem tariff on such articles imported 
    93                  from most countries. In Proclamation 10895 of February 
    94                  10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Aluminum Into the United 
    95                  States), I decided to adjust the imports of aluminum 
    96                  articles and derivative aluminum articles by imposing a 
    97                  25 percent ad valorem tariff on such articles imported 
    98                  from all countries.
    99  
   100                  5. In Proclamation 10896 and Proclamation 10895, I 
   101                  instructed the Secretary to continue to monitor imports 
   102                  of steel articles and derivative steel articles, and 
   103                  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles, 
   104                  respectively, and
   105  
   106  [[Page 24200]]
   107  
   108                  to review the status of such imports with respect to 
   109                  the national security of the United States. The 
   110                  Secretary has done so and has advised me accordingly.
   111  
   112                  6. After considering current information newly provided 
   113                  by the Secretary, among other things, I have determined 
   114                  that it is necessary to increase the previously 
   115                  described steel and aluminum tariffs to adjust the 
   116                  imports of steel and aluminum articles and their 
   117                  derivative articles so that such imports will not 
   118                  threaten to impair the national security. In my 
   119                  judgment, the increased tariffs will more effectively 
   120                  counter foreign countries that continue to offload low-
   121                  priced, excess steel and aluminum in the United States 
   122                  market and thereby undercut the competitiveness of the 
   123                  United States steel and aluminum industries. Although 
   124                  the previously imposed steel and aluminum tariffs have 
   125                  helped provide critical price support in the United 
   126                  States market, they have not yet enabled these 
   127                  industries to develop and maintain the rates of 
   128                  capacity production utilization that are necessary for 
   129                  the industries' sustained health and for projected 
   130                  national defense needs. I have determined that 
   131                  increasing the previously imposed tariffs will provide 
   132                  greater support to these industries and reduce or 
   133                  eliminate the national security threat posed by imports 
   134                  of steel and aluminum articles and their derivative 
   135                  articles.
   136  
   137                  7. Accordingly, I have determined that it is necessary 
   138                  and appropriate to increase the tariff rate for imports 
   139                  of steel articles and derivative steel articles, and 
   140                  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles, 
   141                  from 25 percent ad valorem to 50 percent ad valorem 
   142                  effective as of 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 
   143                  June 4, 2025. I have also determined that it is 
   144                  necessary and appropriate to modify the way in which 
   145                  the tariff measures described in Executive Order 14289 
   146                  of April 29, 2025 (Addressing Certain Tariffs on 
   147                  Imported Articles), apply to steel articles and 
   148                  derivative steel articles, and aluminum articles and 
   149                  derivative aluminum articles, to ensure the 
   150                  effectiveness of the tariff changes described in this 
   151                  proclamation and the alignment of policy priorities 
   152                  between this proclamation and Executive Order 14289. I 
   153                  have further determined that it is necessary and 
   154                  appropriate to allow for the implementation of the 
   155                  U.S.-UK Economic Prosperity Deal of May 8, 2025 (EPD), 
   156                  and to accordingly provide different treatment, as 
   157                  described below, for imports of steel and aluminum 
   158                  articles, and their derivatives, from the United 
   159                  Kingdom.
   160  
   161                  8. Section 232 authorizes the President to adjust the 
   162                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   163                  being imported into the United States in such 
   164                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   165                  to impair the national security.
   166  
   167                  9. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
   168                  U.S.C. 2483), authorizes the President to embody in the 
   169                  Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) 
   170                  the substance of statutes affecting import treatment,

   173                  duty or other import restriction.
   174

   184                      (1) As set forth in Annexes I and II to this 
   185                  proclamation, as of 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 
   186                  June 4, 2025, the tariffs proclaimed by Proclamation 
   187                  9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; 
   188                  Proclamation 9980, as amended; Proclamation 10895; and 
   189                  Proclamation 10896 are modified to increase the 
   190                  respective tariff rates from an additional 25 percent 
   191                  ad valorem to an additional 50 percent ad valorem.
   192                      (2) The modifications to the HTSUS made by clause 1 
   193                  of this proclamation shall be effective with respect to

    23                  Proclamation 11021 of April 2, 2026
    24  
    25                  
    26  Strengthening Actions Taken To Adjust Imports of 
    27                  Aluminum, Steel, and Copper Into the United States
    28  
    29                  By the President of the United States of America
    30  
    31                  A Proclamation
    32  
    33                  1. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    34                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), as 
    35                  amended; Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    36                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), as amended; 
    37                  and Proclamation 10962 of July 30, 2025 (Adjusting 
    38                  Imports of Copper Into the United States), I found, 
    39                  under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, 
    40                  as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1862 (section 232), that 
    41                  aluminum, steel, and copper are being imported into the 
    42                  United States in such quantities or under such 
    43                  circumstances as to threaten to impair the national 
    44                  security of the United States and took action under 
    45                  section 232 to adjust imports of aluminum, steel, and 
    46                  copper articles and their derivative articles 
    47                  (collectively, metal products) so that such imports 
    48                  will not threaten to impair the national security. 
    49                  Specifically, to address the national security threats 
    50                  found in Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and 
    51                  Proclamation 10962, I established tariff regimes, which 
    52                  included imposing additional ad valorem duties on 
    53                  certain imports of metal products.
    54  
    55                  2. In those actions, I also directed the Secretary of 
    56                  Commerce (Secretary) to establish a process for 
    57                  including additional metal products within the scope of 
    58                  the additional ad valorem duties imposed in 
    59                  Proclamation 9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as 
    60                  amended; and Proclamation 10962 and authorized the 
    61                  Secretary to include additional derivative articles 
    62                  within the scope of the duties when the Secretary 
    63                  determined that imports of such products are 
    64                  threatening to impair the national security or 
    65                  otherwise undermining the objectives of the actions 
    66                  taken to address the national security threats found in 
    67                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
    68                  10962. I also instructed the Secretary to monitor the 
    69                  effects of imports of metal products on the national 
    70                  security, to update me on the status of those threats 
    71                  to the national security, and to provide me with 
    72                  recommendations if circumstances indicated the need for 
    73                  further Presidential action under section 232.
    74  
    75                  3. Based on the Secretary's monitoring, I have received 
    76                  information, opinions, and recommendations from the 
    77                  Secretary regarding the tariff regimes imposed in 
    78                  Proclamation 9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as 
    79                  amended; and Proclamation 10962 and the national 
    80                  security threats found in those proclamations.
    81  
    82                  4. Among other things, the Secretary has informed me 
    83                  that the additional ad valorem duties on imports of 
    84                  metal products are strengthening the American aluminum, 
    85                  steel, and copper industries and addressing the 
    86                  national security threats found in Proclamation 9704, 
    87                  Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962. The 
    88                  operation of the aluminum and steel tariff regimes has 
    89                  also improved because of the actions taken in 
    90                  Proclamation 10895 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting 
    91                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), 
    92                  Proclamation 10896 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting 
    93                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), and 
    94                  Proclamation 10947 of June 3, 2025 (Adjusting Imports 
    95                  of Aluminum and Steel Into the United States), which 
    96                  increased the additional ad valorem rate of duty and 
    97                  eliminated loopholes and exemptions in the
    98  
    99  [[Page 18202]]
   100  
   101                  aluminum and steel tariff regimes. For example, under 
   102                  the aluminum and steel tariff regimes, domestic 
   103                  capacity utilization has increased from approximately 
   104                  39 percent in 2017 to approximately 50.4 percent at 
   105                  present for aluminum production and from approximately 
   106                  72.3 percent in 2017 to approximately 77.2 percent at 
   107                  present for steel production, which is closer to the 
   108                  Secretary's recommended objective of achieving a 
   109                  sustained domestic capacity utilization of 80 percent 
   110                  for aluminum and steel production. In the Secretary's 
   111                  opinion, the domestic capacity utilization for aluminum 
   112                  and steel production would not be as high as it is if 
   113                  not for the aluminum and steel tariff regimes imposed 
   114                  under section 232.
   115  
   116                  5. Based on his monitoring of imports of metal 
   117                  products, the Secretary informed me that there are 
   118                  opportunities to continue to improve the operation of 
   119                  the tariff regimes to address more effectively the 
   120                  national security threats found in Proclamation 9704, 
   121                  Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962. For example, 
   122                  the Secretary recommended that I clarify that ad 
   123                  valorem tariffs apply to the full customs value of 
   124                  metal articles, and he recommended that the tariffs 
   125                  apply to the full customs value of derivative products.
   126  
   127                  6. The Secretary further recommended that I modify the 
   128                  scope of derivative articles that are subject to the 
   129                  tariffs imposed under Proclamation 9704 and 
   130                  Proclamation 9705. In the Secretary's view, certain 
   131                  derivative articles should remain subject to the 
   132                  tariffs imposed under Proclamation 9704, as amended, 
   133                  and Proclamation 9705, as amended, to prevent 
   134                  circumvention of the tariffs on aluminum or steel 
   135                  articles or because the derivative article sufficiently 
   136                  contributes to the applicable national security threat 
   137                  found in Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9705. By 
   138                  contrast, in the Secretary's view, other derivative 
   139                  articles should no longer be subject to the tariffs 
   140                  imposed under Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9705 
   141                  because continuing the tariffs does not at this time 
   142                  make a significant contribution to effectively 
   143                  addressing the identified national security threats.
   144  
   145                  7. After considering the current information, opinions, 
   146                  and recommendations newly provided by the Secretary; 
   147                  the factors in section 232 (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)); the 
   148                  need to address the national security threats found in 
   149                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
   150                  10962; and other relevant factors and information, I 
   151                  determine that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   152                  modify, as further described below, the tariff regimes 
   153                  for metal products imposed in Proclamation 9704, as 
   154                  amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; and 
   155                  Proclamation 10962.
   156  
   157                  8. I determine that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   158                  modify the tariffs imposed pursuant to Proclamation 
   159                  9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; and 
   160                  Proclamation 10962 so that they apply to the full 
   161                  customs value of aluminum, steel, and copper articles 
   162                  and their derivatives, regardless of metal content.
   163  
   164                  9. The full-value ad valorem tariffs on aluminum and 
   165                  steel articles, certain copper articles, and certain 
   166                  aluminum and steel derivative articles shall be set at 
   167                  an ad valorem rate of duty of 50 percent, with reduced 
   168                  rates available for certain products from the United 
   169                  Kingdom given the ongoing discussions and for 
   170                  derivative articles made entirely with metals 
   171                  originating from the United States. Full-value tariffs 
   172                  on certain copper articles and certain aluminum and 
   173                  steel derivative articles shall generally be set at an 
   174                  ad valorem rate of duty of 25 percent, with reduced 
   175                  rates available for certain derivative articles from 
   176                  the United Kingdom given the ongoing discussions 
   177                  between the United Kingdom and the United States and 
   178                  for derivative articles made entirely with metals 
   179                  originating from the United States.
   180  
   181                  10. I further determine that it is necessary and 
   182                  appropriate to terminate the aluminum, steel, and 
   183                  copper derivatives inclusions processes established in 
   184                  Proclamation 10895, Proclamation 10896, and 
   185                  Proclamation 10962. I authorize the Secretary and the 
   186                  United States Trade Representative (Trade 
   187                  Representative) to include additional derivative 
   188                  articles within the scope of the tariffs, on a rolling 
   189                  basis, when they jointly determine that imports of 
   190                  those derivative articles threaten to undermine the 
   191                  actions taken to address
   192  
   193  [[Page 18203]]
   194  
   195                  the national security risks identified in Proclamation 
   196                  9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962. In 
   197                  determining whether to include additional derivative 
   198                  articles within the scope of the tariffs, the Secretary 
   199                  and the Trade Representative may solicit information, 
   200                  feedback, recommendations, or other relevant materials 
   201                  from domestic producers, industry associations, or 
   202                  other interested parties.
   203  
   204                  11. I also determine that it is necessary and 
   205                  appropriate to modify the scope of derivative articles 
   206                  subject to tariffs pursuant to Proclamation 9704, as 
   207                  amended, and Proclamation 9705, as amended. These 
   208                  determinations are based on new information and 
   209                  recommendations provided by the Secretary on whether a 
   210                  derivative article sufficiently contributes to the 
   211                  applicable national security threats found in 
   212                  Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9705, whether 
   213                  imposing tariffs on the derivative article is necessary 
   214                  to prevent circumvention of the tariffs on steel or 
   215                  aluminum articles, and whether a tariff on the full 
   216                  customs value of the derivative article will enable the 
   217                  tariff regimes, at this time, to address as effectively 
   218                  the national security threats found in Proclamation 
   219                  9704 and Proclamation 9705.
   220  
   221                  12. In my judgment, the modifications in this 
   222                  proclamation are necessary and appropriate to adjust 
   223                  imports of metal products to address more effectively 
   224                  the threats to the national security found in 
   225                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
   226                  10962, including by, among other things, more 
   227                  effectively and quickly strengthening domestic 
   228                  manufacturing of metal products; reducing reliance on 
   229                  foreign manufacturing and importation of metal 
   230                  products; encouraging companies to expand domestic 
   231                  production capacity of metal products; increasing 
   232                  domestic research and development of metal products so 
   233                  that United States producers can produce cutting-edge 
   234                  technologies that are essential to the United States 
   235                  defense industrial base; and training workers to 
   236                  produce these strategic products.
   237  
   238                  13. Section 232 authorizes the President to adjust the 
   239                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   240                  being imported into the United States in such 
   241                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   242                  to impair the national security of the United States so 
   243                  that such imports will not threaten to impair the 
   244                  national security.
   245  
   246                  14. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended 
   247                  (19 U.S.C. 2483) (section 604), authorizes the 
   248                  President to embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule 
   249                  of the United States (HTSUS) the substance of statutes 
   250                  affecting import treatment, and actions thereunder, 
   251                  including the removal, modification, continuance, or 
   252                  imposition of any rate of duty or other import 
   253                  restriction.
   254  
   255                  NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the 
   256                  United States of America, by the authority vested in me 
   257                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, 
   258                  including section 232, section 604, and section 301 of 
   259                  title 3, United States Code, do hereby proclaim as 
   260                  follows:

    60                  of Aluminum, Steel, and Copper Into the United States
    61  
    62                  By the President of the United States of America
    63  
    64                  A Proclamation
    65  
    66                  1. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    67                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), as 
    68                  amended; Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    69                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), as amended; 
    70                  and Proclamation 10962 of July 30, 2025 (Adjusting 
    71                  Imports of Copper Into the United States), as amended, 
    72                  I found, under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act 
    73                  of 1962, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1862 (section 232), that 
    74                  aluminum, steel, and copper are being imported into the 
    75                  United States in such quantities or under such 
    76                  circumstances as to threaten to impair the national 
    77                  security of the United States and took action under 
    78                  section 232 to adjust imports of aluminum, steel, and 
    79                  copper articles and their derivative articles 
    80                  (collectively, metal products) so that such imports 
    81                  will not threaten to impair the national security. 
    82                  Specifically, to address the national security threats 
    83                  found in Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and 
    84                  Proclamation 10962, I established tariff regimes, which 
    85                  included imposing additional ad valorem duties on 
    86                  certain imports of metal products.
    87  
    88                  2. In Proclamation 11021 of April 2, 2026 
    89                  (Strengthening Actions Taken To Adjust Imports of 
    90                  Aluminum, Steel, and Copper Into the United States), I 
    91                  modified the tariff regimes established under section 
    92                  232 for imports of metal products to more effectively 
    93                  address the national security threats found in 
    94                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
    95                  10962. In particular, I imposed an ad valorem duty of 
    96                  50 percent on products made of those metals; an ad 
    97                  valorem duty of 25 percent on derivative products that 
    98                  tend to be predominately composed of those metals; and 
    99                  a temporarily-reduced ad valorem duty of 15 percent on 
   100                  a subset of derivative products, namely fixed 
   101                  industrial machinery and power equipment.
   102  
   103                  3. Based on the Secretary of Commerce's (Secretary) 
   104                  monitoring and consultation with other senior 
   105                  officials, among other things, the Secretary has 
   106                  provided me information, opinions, and recommendations 
   107                  regarding the tariff regimes imposed in Proclamation 
   108                  9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; and 
   109                  Proclamation 10962, as amended, and the national 
   110                  security threats found in those proclamations. Among 
   111                  other things, the Secretary has informed me that recent 
   112                  circumstances have affected and are affecting domestic 
   113                  industries that use agricultural equipment, industrial 
   114                  equipment and machinery, and other related products. 
   115                  Many products in these categories are treated as 
   116                  derivative articles of aluminum or steel because they 
   117                  tend to be predominantly composed of aluminum or steel. 
   118                  These products also serve an important role in 
   119                  productive domestic economic activity. For example, 
   120                  American farmers use agricultural equipment to produce 
   121                  the food upon which our Nation relies; construction 
   122                  equipment is essential for the continued 
   123                  reindustrialization of our Nation; and material-
   124                  handling equipment enables industrial logistics and 
   125                  factory operations.
   126  
   127                  4. To account for these circumstances, the Secretary 
   128                  recommended that I modify the tariffs imposed on these 
   129                  products pursuant to Proclamation 9704, as amended, and 
   130                  Proclamation 9705, as amended. In particular, the 
   131                  Secretary recommended that I expand the category of 
   132                  derivative products
   133  
   134  [[Page 34086]]
   135  
   136                  subject to the temporarily-reduced 15 percent ad 
   137                  valorem duty to include agricultural equipment and 
   138                  certain heating, ventilation, and air conditioning 
   139                  (HVAC) systems and components that are predominately 
   140                  for residential use, which are currently treated as 
   141                  aluminum or steel derivative products. The Secretary 
   142                  also recommended that I temporarily modify the tariffs 
   143                  imposed on mobile industrial equipment and machinery to 
   144                  support the American businesses and factories that use 
   145                  these products.
   146  
   147                  5. In addition, the Secretary has recommended that I 
   148                  include two types of aluminum and steel products 
   149                  (aluminum lithographic plates and steel racks) that are 
   150                  not currently subject to aluminum and steel tariffs 
   151                  within the product coverage of Proclamation 11021, to 
   152                  ensure that they are subject to the appropriate tariffs 
   153                  for aluminum and steel derivative products and to 
   154                  ensure that the purpose of the tariff regimes to 
   155                  address the national security threats found in 
   156                  Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 9705 are not 
   157                  undermined. The Secretary also recommended that I 
   158                  modify the threshold for imported products to qualify 
   159                  as made ``entirely'' from American aluminum, steel, or 
   160                  copper, as that term is used in Proclamation 11021.
   161  
   162                  6. After considering the current information, opinions, 
   163                  and recommendations newly provided by the Secretary; 
   164                  the factors in section 232 (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)); the 
   165                  need to address the national security threats found in 
   166                  Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 
   167                  10962; and other relevant factors and information, I 
   168                  determine that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   169                  modify, as further described below, the tariff regimes 
   170                  for metal products imposed in Proclamation 9704, as 
   171                  amended, Proclamation 9705, as amended, and 
   172                  Proclamation 10962, as amended.
   173  
   174                  7. I determine that agricultural equipment and certain 
   175                  HVAC systems and components that are predominantly for 
   176                  residential use shall be included in the category of 
   177                  derivative products subject to the temporarily-reduced 
   178                  15 percent ad valorem duty under Proclamation 11021. In 
   179                  my judgment, this modification appropriately accounts 
   180                  for these products' roles in productive economic 
   181                  activity in the United States and accounts for recent 
   182                  circumstances affecting the relevant industries and 
   183                  services that use these products, while also enabling 
   184                  the tariff regimes to continue effectively addressing 
   185                  the national security threats found in Proclamation 
   186                  9704 and Proclamation 9705.
   187  
   188                  8. I determine that it is necessary and appropriate to 
   189                  temporarily modify the tariffs imposed on mobile 
   190                  industrial equipment and machinery, as detailed below. 
   191                  In my judgment, this temporary modification 
   192                  appropriately accounts for these products' roles in 
   193                  productive economic activity in the United States and 
   194                  accounts for recent circumstances affecting the 
   195                  relevant industries and services that use these 
   196                  products, while also allowing the tariff regimes to 
   197                  continue effectively addressing the national security 
   198                  threats found in Proclamation 9704 and Proclamation 
   199                  9705.
   200  
   201                  9. I determine that aluminum lithographic plates and 
   202                  steel racks constitute aluminum and steel derivative 
   203                  products that should be subject to the applicable 
   204                  derivative tariff under Proclamation 11021. In my 
   205                  judgment, subjecting these products to the derivative 
   206                  tariff in Proclamation 11021 will ensure that the 
   207                  tariffs on metal products are not circumvented and that 
   208                  the purpose of the actions to address the national 
   209                  security threats found in Proclamation 9704 and 
   210                  Proclamation 9705 is not undermined.
   211  
   212                  10. I determine that it is appropriate to modify the 
   213                  threshold for imported products to qualify as made 
   214                  ``entirely'' from American aluminum, steel, or copper, 
   215                  as that term is used in Proclamation 11021. The current 
   216                  threshold of 95 percent shall be modified to 85 
   217                  percent. In my judgment, this modification will 
   218                  incentivize increased use of American aluminum, steel, 
   219                  and copper in downstream derivative products and 
   220                  further the purpose of the actions to address the 
   221                  national security threats found in Proclamation 9704, 
   222                  Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962.
   223  
   224  [[Page 34087]]
   225  
   226                  11. Section 232 authorizes the President to adjust the 
   227                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   228                  being imported into the United States in such 
   229                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   230                  to impair the national security of the United States so 
   231                  that such imports will not threaten to impair the 
   232                  national security.
   233  
   234                  12. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended, 
   235                  19 U.S.C. 2483 (section 604), authorizes the President 
   236                  to embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the 
   237                  United States (HTSUS) the substance of statutes 
   238                  affecting import treatment, and actions thereunder, 
   239                  including the removal, modification, continuance, or 
   240                  imposition of any rate of duty or other import 
   241                  restriction.
   242

summary.text:
**Analyzing tariff treatment**

I’m working through the treatment of Canadian mobile industrial machinery under Section 232 and the relevant annexes. The key facts are that the machinery appears in Annex I-C, most of its metal is not U.S.-origin, and it entered with a USMCA preference claim.

I’m checking the June proclamation’s clauses and the later 2026 annex materials to determine whether the applicable rate is 25% or 50%. The central issue is whether the USMCA rule limits the tariff to the product’s non-U.S. steel and aluminum content, along with any exception for entirely U.S.-origin metal.

summary.text:
**Calculating tariff treatments**

I’m parsing how clause 2(d) applies to non-U.S. content and checking the 15% effective-duty floor. For a Canadian USMCA machine with $140,000 in non-U.S. content, 25% produces $35,000, or 17.5% of the $200,000 value, so the floor doesn’t change the result. With no U.S. content, the duty is $50,000. A non-USMCA machine also appears subject to 25%. For Japan, if the MFN rate is 2.5%, the additional rate would be 12.5% to reach 15%, assuming the listed-country provision controls.**Interpreting duty provisions**

I’m separating the Section 232 amount from any other applicable charge, giving $25,000 for the stated case. In the next scenario, I’m treating only U.S.-made parts as excluded from the non-U.S. content calculation. That leaves $180,000 subject to 25%, or $45,000, which exceeds the 15% floor. I’m also checking whether the special 10% rule applies: it appears limited to qualifying derivative articles with entirely U.S.-processed metal, while the scenario describes a listed steel article, so classification remains important.

**Evaluating material-origin rules**

I’m distinguishing between material smelted or cast in the United States and parts actually produced here. Because most of the steel and aluminum is sourced outside the United States by weight, the provision treating the material as entirely domestic does not apply. The $30,000 of U.S.-processed aluminum inside a foreign-made part therefore cannot be counted as a U.S.-produced part. I’m calculating non-U.S. content as total value minus qualifying U.S.-produced parts, yielding $180,000, or $45,000 at 25%. I’m also checking whether the October 6 entry predates the June 8 effective date.**Checking effective dates**

I’m revisiting the timeline because the October 6 entry date appears to fall after the June 8, 2026 changes. If the scenario distinguishes parts (e) and (f), there may be a temporary rate period or special treatment for the machinery category involved. I need to verify whether the relevant schedule covers mobile or fixed industrial equipment and whether any temporary provision expires around October 15. The exact date and applicable annex classification could materially change the calculation.

I’m interpreting Q13 as applying the June 2026 proclamation’s Annex I-C rates to the mobile machine. Because the machine is classified as a steel article in that annex, the non-USMCA rate appears to be 25%. On that reading, the 25% duty applies to $180,000, producing $45,000. I’m still checking why October 6 matters.**Clarifying the October date**

The proclamation’s preamble may refer to a temporary machinery modification whose precise details appear only in an image-based annex. Since those terms are uncertain, I shouldn’t confidently apply a separate machinery rate without the annex text.

The main text appears to establish a baseline rule for products listed in Annex I-C, while Annex IV may provide machine-specific rates for defined periods. The dates in the question likely test whether a temporary timing provision remains effective. I’m checking whether another October 2026 proclamation modifies the applicable steel or aluminum rates.**Searching relevant terms**

summary.text:
**Interpreting tariff provisions**

I’m reading the provisions as distinguishing several annexes: 11021 appears to address Annexes I-A, I-B, and III, while 11032 adds Annex I-C. Clause 3 of 11021 seems to establish a 25% rate for Annex I-B products, with separate exceptions or adjustments. For Annex I-C goods, 11032 clause 3(a) appears effective January 1, 2028, by incorporating the 11021 clause 3 rate. The Canada-specific treatment seems clearer only through December 31, 2027; afterward, the exact treatment of Canadian content remains uncertain.**Clarifying the timeline**

I’m treating December 31, 2027, as the endpoint for the current special treatment. Starting January 1, 2028, clause 3(a) shifts the applicable additional rate to the rate established under clause 3 of 11021. The precise amount still depends on the product’s listing and the provenance of its metal inputs. For a predominantly foreign product made in Canada, the likely result is the baseline rate applied to the full customs value, unless a specific annex or de minimis rule changes that outcome.

summary.text:
**Interpreting tariff treatment**

I’m reading the provision as keeping the USMCA treatment for Canada’s non-U.S. content at 25% through December 31, 2027. After that date, the language appears to shift to the rate in clause (3) of Proclamation 11021.

Because the machine is mostly made with non-U.S. metal and no approved onshoring-plan exception applies, my best reading is a 25% rate on the full customs value rather than a content-adjusted amount. I’m treating the Annex I-C classification as subject to that later clause, even though the proclamation does not add a new Annex I-C.**Assessing missing rate details**

I’m noticing that the stated onshoring program appears irrelevant because it covers only primary aluminum, while this machine is not covered. The dates may matter if Annex IV created a special rate for mobile equipment, but the available text does not show that table or formula.

I also can’t apply the 85%-weight rule because most of the machine’s metal is not U.S.-origin. Therefore, I can state the general treatment, but I can’t determine the exact duty confidently without Annex IV. If no special benefit applies, the stated base calculation would be $45,000.

**Calculating tariff treatment**

I’m applying the stated rate assumptions to the readable note. For aloe products under 1302.19.91, Cambodia appears exempt under item 9903.06.03, while Malaysia has no matching exemption identified in the text. I’m therefore treating Malaysia’s aloe shipment as subject to the 10% rate, or $6,000.

For Boswellia, Malaysia appears exempt under 9903.06.01. Taiwan doesn’t appear to have a comparable personal exemption, so I’m applying the 10% rate, assuming the product isn’t covered by a separate annex-specific exclusion.**Checking negotiated exemptions**

I’m reconsidering Taiwan’s Boswellia treatment because it may have a separate negotiated exemption in an annex, but the relevant image is unreadable. The available text doesn’t establish whether that product is covered. I’m therefore looking for explicit entries for Boswellia, argan, sesame, and psyllium, while comparing the country-specific provisions already identified for Malaysia, Cambodia, Guatemala, Jordan, and Taiwan. Until the Taiwan entry is confirmed, I shouldn’t treat the 10% rate as definitive.

summary.text:
**Assessing product carveouts**

I’m reviewing the Q12 tariff treatment country by country. Cambodia appears excluded under the cited provision, while Malaysia’s aloe product may still face the listed tariff unless Annex II Part E specifically exempts the relevant subheading. I’m checking whether “herbal extracts” could cover it, but the available excerpt doesn’t identify aloe directly. The scenario’s general assumption about annex-listed products is ambiguous here, so I shouldn’t infer that Q12’s products qualify without an explicit statement.

**Reviewing tariff treatment**

I’m applying the list across all economies, so Japan, Mexico, and Thailand receive zero for sesame seeds for sowing because the relevant classification is specifically exempted.

For psyllium, Cambodia appears exempt under its designated provision. Thailand does not seem to qualify for an exemption, so I’m applying the default 12.5% rate, or $5,000. El Salvador may require checking an additional exclusion provision before finalizing. Italy’s 2% MFN rate rises to a 10% target, producing an 8% additional duty, or $3,200 on $40,000.**Checking psyllium rates**

I’m treating the EU Annex II exemption as uncertain because it may not cover every psyllium product. For Italy, I’m therefore using the general 2% rate against a 10% target, leaving an 8% additional duty. For Thailand, the default 12.5% rate gives $5,000. El Salvador appears to have a general 10% rate, but I still need to verify whether a specific text-based exemption applies by reviewing the relevant provisions around the identified section.

summary.text:
**Clarifying trade claims**

I’m calculating the psyllium figures using the stated 10% assumption for El Salvador and 8% for Italy, while noting that Q13(f) lacks a precise answer.

For Q14, I’m separating the memorandum’s operative language from its explanatory text. The memorandum instructs USTR to act “as soon as” feasibility is determined, rather than imposing a firm September 1 deadline; the September date appears in the surrounding explanation. The claim about more than 450 written submissions and nearly 60 witnesses is accurate for the earlier proceeding, while the later proposal received substantially more participation.**Assessing comment figures**

I’m distinguishing the initial investigation from the later proposed-action proceeding. The figures of more than 450 written comments and nearly 60 witnesses belong to the earlier investigation, so attributing them to comments on the proposal is inaccurate, even though the numbers themselves are documented.

The claim about seven economies moving from 12.5% to 10% because each adopted an import ban also appears overstated. The relevant economies had different commitments and classifications; some were linked to proposed arrangements rather than newly adopted bans.

**Clarifying rate changes**

I’m sorting out which economies actually shifted from 12.5% to 10%. Cambodia and Guatemala already appeared at 10% through their negotiated commitments, so I shouldn’t count them as reductions. The clearest five reductions are Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago, and Jordan. Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, and Trinidad and Tobago appear tied to newly adopted import prohibitions, while Jordan’s change comes through an undertaking. I’m treating this as the more precise interpretation of the final memo.**Correcting memo details**

I’m revising several claims. The memo identifies seven economies associated with new actions—six import bans plus Jordan’s undertaking—but only five appear to move from 12.5% to 10%, since Cambodia and Guatemala were already proposed at 10%. I’m also correcting the product-exemption point: beef and avocados remained exempt, despite comments urging their removal. Finally, I shouldn’t say every economy received its own negotiated list. The additional country-specific lists apply to the EU, Switzerland, and Taiwan; Japan and South Korea receive only the common exceptions.

**Evaluating tariff claims**

I’m checking each statement against the notice. There is no dedicated Japan or South Korea section; instead, I’m using the table of contents and investigation references for those economies.

The claim about 471 additional product classifications is partly correct: the number applies within each investigation, not collectively. The notice adds certain sugar and sugar-containing products, not all such products.

The claim that no product bears more than 12.5% overall is incorrect. The notice describes additional rates, while most-favored-nation duties may apply separately, so the combined total can exceed 12.5%.**Checking remaining provisions**

I’m confirming that the annex describes additional duties layered onto existing most-favored-nation rates. The 12.5% figure is not a universal ceiling: some countries receive a net-of-MFN calculation, while others can exceed that combined level.

The foreign-trade-zone statement appears correct, subject to the notice’s specific treatment of privileged foreign status and any applicable domestic-status exception. The severability claim is also broadly accurate: if a particular exemption is invalidated, the affected goods may become dutiable, without automatically invalidating unrelated exemptions.

The final claim concerns whether only certain chemicals receive reductions.

**Comparing trade documents**

I’m checking whether the statement accurately reflects the USTR description. It appears correct, with one important qualification: the exemption applies to nonpharmaceutical uses of certain chemicals, not necessarily to all chemical products.

I’m also looking for inconsistencies between the two documents. One possible difference concerns textiles: the proposal described a reduced Section 301 tariff rate, while the final memorandum established tariff-free treatment within quotas. That may reflect a change between proposal and implementation rather than an error in the reporting.**Checking document consistency**

I’m finding that most details align across the presidential memorandum and the USTR notice. The reported number of public comments and witnesses is consistent, and the projected September 1, 2026 date for tariff-rate quotas appears to be an implementation estimate rather than a contradiction.

The country-specific tariff rates and listed negotiated exemptions also generally match. The references to annexes differ in presentation, but not apparently in effect. I’m still checking whether South Korea’s stated net MFN rate creates a substantive discrepancy, though the documents currently appear consistent.

**Comparing scope statements**

I'm checking whether the notice's introductory description of proposed exemptions matches the operative text. The introduction appears to describe the proposal as covering all articles and parts subject to Section 232, while the adopted U.S. note seems to exempt only specified categories. I’m distinguishing the proposal from the final rule rather than treating them as contradictory automatically.

The key question is whether the preamble later claims that all proposed products were exempted, apart from limited chemical exceptions. I’m comparing that language with the Annex I footnote and effective-date provisions to identify any genuine inconsistency.**Reconciling tariff language**

I'm checking whether the notice's description of a 10% tariff on Canadian products overlooks the USMCA treatment. The operative note appears to preserve duty-free treatment for qualifying USMCA goods, and because that exception is included in Annex I, the summary's reference to Annex I and II exemptions may still be accurate.

I'm also comparing the notice's in-transit transition rule—covering goods loaded before July 24 and entered before July 28—with the corresponding HTSUS language. The next step is verifying whether the operative provisions reproduce that exception precisely.

summary.text:
**Comparing tariff exceptions**

I’m checking whether the documents align on several points. The DATES line appears to contain an exception, while the U.S. note does not mention transit; that may simply reflect separate import rules rather than a contradiction.

The memorandum creates tariff-rate quotas for certain textile and cotton imports, with a temporary 10% rate until those quotas are established.

The clearer discrepancy concerns personal-use baggage: the operative notice expressly exempts accompanied baggage, but the memorandum’s general tariff language and annex do not state that exception.**Assessing baggage treatment**

I’m revisiting the personal-use baggage issue. The operative notice exempts accompanied baggage, while the memorandum directs tariffs on all covered products and does not expressly identify baggage as an exception. Because baggage is not necessarily a standard product heading, the annex’s product list may not resolve this ambiguity.

My cautious conclusion is that this is best described as a possible implementation difference, not a direct contradiction. The notice may provide additional relief beyond what the memorandum clearly states. The textile and cotton quota language, by contrast, appears consistent across both documents.

**Comparing tariff exemptions**

I’m checking whether the memorandum and adopted tariff text align. The Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia language appears consistent, including the tariff-rate-quota treatment and rate cap.

The main issue is exemption scope. The July notice describes exemptions from the proposal, including informational materials, donations, baggage, and Section 232 goods. However, the adopted text appears narrower: it expressly addresses accompanied baggage but does not generally exempt informational materials, donations, or all Section 232 goods. I’m therefore distinguishing proposed language from the final adopted provisions.**Checking procedural consistency**

I’m reviewing whether the summary accurately characterizes the preamble and rate provisions. The exemption language should remain qualified rather than implying broad categorical exclusions, and the treatment of forced-labor import prohibitions appears generally rate-dependent.

The more significant issue is timing. The initial proclamations state an August 19 effective date, while a later amendment changes Annex II to August 22 but leaves some operative clauses referring to August 19. Later materials explain the three-day suspension, so I’m treating this as an internal date inconsistency worth identifying separately.

**Comparing operative provisions**

I’m finding that the source document remains unchanged and that this is the same apparent mismatch. The recitals in Proclamations 11064 and 11065 say the suspension lapsed at 12:01 a.m. on August 22, making duties effective. Proclamation 11056 likewise makes the duties effective August 22, suspends collection where required, and provides for refunds, so I’m not seeing a contradiction.

The 30-day timing is worth noting: the original effective date was exactly 30 days after the July 20 signing, while the amended date was 33 days later. Later adjustments occurred sooner after signing, but that alone doesn’t establish a discrepancy.**Assessing apparent discrepancies**

I’m treating the seven-day effective dates for later scope expansions as potentially confusing, but not necessarily inconsistent: the 30-day requirement can reasonably be measured from the initial July 20 finding. I’ll note that the later proclamations don’t clearly explain this relationship.

The product-scope provisions otherwise appear aligned. One proclamation removes certain products from coverage, while another clarifies that the change does not otherwise alter the established scope. The transition rules also distinguish prohibited imports from previously imported goods awaiting entry. I’m not seeing a general factual mismatch, including for listed exclusions.

**Reconciling duty provisions**

I’m comparing the earlier proclamations with the later September scope language. The initial provision exempts articles already subject to Section 232 duties, while the later text says the modified duties apply in addition to Section 232 duties.

That appears to be an intentional subsequent modification rather than a simple inconsistency: the newer operative language likely controls over the earlier exclusion. I’m also noting that the September provisions cover goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouses, while the recitals identify an August 22 effective date.**Assessing amendment conflicts**

I’m treating the September language as an intentional later modification, not an internal contradiction. Its recitals describe the original duty and subsequent modification, while the operative text states that the duties apply in addition to Section 232 duties.

Still, because the earlier exclusion remains visible and is not expressly amended paragraph-by-paragraph, I should flag this as a cross-document conflict: the newer operative provision likely controls, but the documents do not fully harmonize. I’m also checking related effective-date and suspension language for separate discrepancies.

**Comparing proclamation dates**

I’m comparing the August 22 and September 29 dates to determine whether they conflict. The apparent difference may simply reflect a later suspension or modification.

Proclamations 11061, 11062, and 11063 paragraph 2 indicate that goods imported before September 29 but not yet entered remain subject to the 50% duty; the exclusion does not retroactively prevent entry. That appears consistent.

Proclamation 11064 takes effect September 15, with one section imposing additional duties and another removing certain products from coverage.**Reviewing scope and tariff history**

I’m checking whether the annex language creates inconsistencies. The October provisions appear coherent: Part A removes products from coverage, while Part B subjects products to duties, with both tied to October 30. The title of Proclamation 11064 is broader than one paragraph, but the annexes and operative text resolve that apparent tension. Preamble statements seem explanatory rather than controlling. For the later history, I’m tracking how the aluminum and steel rates changed and whether the product remained in Annex I-A rather than moving into the special Annex I-C regime.

**Clarifying tariff assumptions**

I’m organizing the tariff assumptions for Q15. From April 6, I’m treating the goods as entered under heading 9903.82.02 at their full customs value. Although a later measure might remove products from a specified list, I’m assuming these remain covered by Annex I-A and subject to 50%.

Because the product is an aluminum extrusion, I’m treating its entire value as aluminum content. That means calculating the duty on metal content or declared value produces the same result. I’m also checking the effective dates and the applicable Section 232 rate before June 4, 2025.

summary.text:
**Evaluating applicable duties**

I’m assessing which additional duties applied to aluminum extrusions from Canada as of the relevant entry date. The key issue is timing: a February 10, 2025 proclamation was signed then but became effective March 12, while Canada was previously exempt under the bilateral Section 232 arrangement. I’m also separating IEEPA measures, Section 232, Section 301, Section 338, reciprocal tariffs, and any temporary surcharge. The central uncertainty is whether later Canada-specific exclusions or USMCA treatment remove a surcharge after IEEPA changes.**Determining surcharge duration**

I’m checking the operative language to confirm how the temporary surcharge interacts with Section 232, Section 301, exclusions, foreign-trade zones, and expiration. For goods entered after the surcharge’s 150-day period, I need to distinguish whether the final covered date is July 23 or July 24, 2026. That timing matters because entries in late July, August, September, and November may fall outside the surcharge. I’m also treating the northern-border IEEPA measure separately because it ended earlier.

summary.text:
**Assessing surcharge treatment**

I’m determining whether the section 122 surcharge applies across the scenarios and entry dates. For the aluminum extrusions, I’m treating section 232 coverage as excluding them under paragraph 14(k), regardless of whether they qualify for USMCA; USMCA qualification would provide an additional exemption under paragraph 14(l). That exclusion applies while section 232 is active. I’m also noting that entries after the surcharge’s stated expiration do not incur it. For the September rye-whisky entry, the surcharge period has ended, so no surcharge applies.**Reviewing tariff timing**

I’m separating the September and historical Q15 scenarios. For September, I’m treating section 301, the Canada IEEPA duties, and the temporary surcharge as inactive, so none applies. For February 10, 2025, I’m noting that the IEEPA measures had not yet taken effect and that Canada’s aluminum arrangement remained relevant. By March 6, I’m recognizing that IEEPA duties had begun, while the USMCA-related exemption had not yet started. The section 232 treatment remains dependent on the stated assumptions about Canada’s aluminum arrangements and coverage.

**Understanding tariff timelines**

I’m mapping how Section 232 treatment for Canadian aluminum changed from 2019 through 2025, focusing on aluminum bars, rods, and profiles under heading 7604. The initial Canada arrangement suspended the tariff, but a retaliatory reimposition may have occurred in August 2020 before later removal.

The dates in question likely test boundary changes: February 10, March 6, March 10, March 14, June 3, June 10, August 5, March 2, July 27, August 25, September 14, September 16, and November 10. I’m distinguishing dates before and after each policy change carefully.**Mapping duty changes**

I’m organizing the dates around overlapping tariff regimes. Canada’s IEEPA rate reaches 25% by March 4, while USMCA treatment becomes available March 7. Section 232 aluminum treatment changes March 12, and the rate rises from 25% to 50% in early June. Later dates require separating USMCA eligibility from Section 232 coverage, since Section 301 may exclude products already covered by Section 232. I’m also checking when Section 338 begins and when its scope changes, especially around August 22 and September 15.

**Reviewing tariff treatment**

I’m tracking how several tariff authorities interact for Canada and motor-related goods. The notes indicate that Section 232 treatment may continue for both categories, while Section 301 is exempt and the IEEPA surcharge has expired. A later framework appears to combine Section 338 and Section 232 duties, with potential scope changes for vehicles or components after September 15.

I’m also checking whether Canadian goods, previously excluded from reciprocal tariffs because of IEEPA-based measures, could become subject to a 10% baseline after those measures ended.**Clarifying reciprocal tariffs**

I’m checking whether the termination order also ends reciprocal tariffs imposed under the separate IEEPA framework. The key issue is whether the termination expressly covers duties created by the earlier reciprocal-tariff order, including any treatment of Canadian goods. My current understanding is that the reciprocal duty would not continue into 2026, while 2025 treatment depended on exemptions for Canadian products and any applicable Section 232 measures. I’m verifying the precise exclusion language before stating this definitively.

summary.text:
**Clarifying tariff chronology**

I’m distinguishing the reciprocal-duty rules from the later termination order. Under the earlier arrangement, qualifying Canadian goods under the USMCA were exempt, while non-qualifying goods could face a 12% rate if the border tariffs were suspended or terminated. However, the later order expressly ended the tariff actions under the earlier order, so the reciprocal 12% provision appears to have ended as well. Before that termination, Canada wasn’t subject to an additional reciprocal tariff. I’m also tracking the separate aluminum timeline, including the February proclamation taking effect March 12, 2025.**Examining aluminum treatment**

I’m checking whether Canadian aluminum imports were covered by the earlier agreement before March 12, 2025. The key issue is whether the 2019 arrangement created a quota, with Section 232 duties applying only to quantities exceeding that limit. For the specified extrusion classification, I need to verify the agreement’s exact scope and quota mechanics. Without evidence that the shipment exceeded a quota, the cautious conclusion is that it was exempt before March 12, though the legal result depends on the product’s quota status and the governing proclamations.

summary.text:
**Assessing aluminum tariffs**

I’m sorting out how the tariff treatment applies to aluminum extrusions under heading 7604. The key change appears to be a 25% increase effective March 12, while prior arrangements may have exempted Canada or applied different Section 232 treatment.

The alternative quota arrangement complicates the conclusion: Canadian imports may remain exempt up to a benchmark, with the tariff returning above that level. Because no quota data is provided, I’m leaning toward stating the documented exemption while clearly noting that the actual duty depends on import volumes and the applicable tariff subheading.**Clarifying quota treatment**

I’m weighing two interpretations. The 2019 Canada arrangement generally allowed tariff-free treatment within annual quota volumes, but the prompt does not specify whether those quota conditions are satisfied. That creates a genuine uncertainty.

However, the stated assumptions may be intended to simplify classification by treating the product as covered by Section 232 throughout the period. I’m therefore checking the precise Canadian agreement and tariff provisions before deciding whether to apply the standard rate, recognize a quota-based exemption, or flag the result as indeterminate without import-volume information.

    69                  1. On January 19, 2018, the Secretary of Commerce

    72                  articles on the national security of the United States 
    73                  under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962,

    82                  concurred in the Secretary's finding that aluminum 
    83                  articles were being imported into the United States in 
    84                  such quantities and under such circumstances as to 
    85                  threaten to impair the national security of the United 
    86                  States, and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum 
    87                  articles, as defined in clause 1 of Proclamation 9704, 
    88                  by imposing a 10 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    89                  articles imported from most countries.

    92                  country with which we have a security relationship is 
    93                  welcome to discuss with the United States alternative 
    94                  ways to address the threatened impairment of the 
    95                  national security caused by imports from that country,

    97                  country arrive at a satisfactory alternative means to 
    98                  address the threat to the national security such that I 
    99                  determine that imports from that country no longer 
   100                  threaten to impair the national security, I may remove 
   101                  or modify the restriction on aluminum articles imports 
   102                  from that country and, if necessary, adjust the tariff 
   103                  as it applies to other countries, as the national 
   104                  security interests of the United States require.
   105  
   106                  4. The United States has successfully concluded 
   107                  discussions with Canada and Mexico on satisfactory 
   108                  alternative means to address the threatened impairment 
   109                  of the national security posed by aluminum imports from

   111                  range of measures with Canada and Mexico to prevent the 
   112                  importation of aluminum that is unfairly subsidized or 
   113                  sold at dumped prices, to prevent the transshipment of

   119                  reasonably commensurate with the target level

   121                  these measures will provide effective, long-term 
   122                  alternative means to address the contribution of these 
   123                  countries' imports to the threatened impairment of the

summary.text:
**Calculating Canadian duties**

I’m determining how Section 232 and IEEPA duties apply to Canadian aluminum extrusions across the listed dates. The product is not non-alloyed unwrought aluminum, so the exclusion ends March 12, 2025; Section 232 is therefore zero beforehand.

For Case N, I’m applying the initial 25% IEEPA rate on March 6 and March 10, while February 10 remains zero. On March 14, I’m adding the 25% Section 232 duty, but I still need to verify whether later stacking rules change the combined amount.**Checking tariff stacking**

I’m assessing whether the duties could be added together on March 14 and June 3. The earlier language appears to allow IEEPA duties in addition to existing tariffs, suggesting a possible combined rate of 50%. For June 10, the apparent total could reach 75% after the Section 232 increase, but that conclusion may be wrong.

A later order issued April 29 may limit stacking when aluminum is already subject to Section 232. I’m verifying that rule before finalizing the calculations.
